entries.cd9f8f25c1ddac0eb0d35e9f77d24b0623d46b2e: <div sID="gen22051" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Matt.11" sID="Matt.11"/> <div eID="gen22051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22052" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22053" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The constant and unwearied diligence of our Lord Jesus in his great work of preaching the gospel, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. His discourse with the disciples of John concerning his being the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6">ver. 2-6</reference>. III. The honourable testimony that Christ bore to John Baptist, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.7-Matt.11.15">ver. 7-15</reference>. IV. The sad account he gives of that generation in general, and of some particular places with reference to the success, both of John's ministry and of his own, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.16-Matt.11.24">ver. 16-24</reference>. V. His thanksgiving to his Father for the wise and gracious method he had taken in revealing the great mysteries of the gospel, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.25-Matt.11.26">ver. 25, 26</reference>. VI. His gracious call and invitation of poor sinners to come to him, and to be ruled, and taught, and saved by him, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27-Matt.11.30">ver. 27-30</reference>. No Where have we more of the terror of gospel woes for warning to us, or of the sweetness of gospel grace for encouragement to us, than in this chapter, which sets before us life and death, the blessing and the curse.
entries.380e8c5ec0734fedfbf0a39dc71c9bad1734faca: <div eID="gen22053" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22052" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">John's Disciples Come to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen22054" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end of commanding his twelve disciples, he departed thence to teach and to preach in their cities. <hi type="super">2</hi> Now when John had heard in the prison the works of Christ, he sent two of his disciples, 3 And said unto him, Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another? <hi type="super">4</hi> Jesus answered and said unto them, Go and show John again those things which ye do hear and see: <hi type="super">5</hi> The blind receive their sight, and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them. <hi type="super">6</hi> And blessed is <hi type="italic">he,</hi> whosoever shall not be offended in me. <div eID="gen22054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> The first verse of this chapter some join to the foregoing chapter, and make it (not unfitly) the close of that. <div eID="gen22055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22056" type="x-p"/> 1. The ordination sermon which Christ preached to his disciples in the foregoing chapter is here called his commanding them. Note, Christ's commissions imply commands. Their preaching of the gospel was not only permitted them, but it was enjoined them. It was not a thing respecting which they were left at their liberty, but <hi type="italic">necessity was laid upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.16">1 Cor. ix. 16</reference>. The promises he made them are included in these commands, for the covenant of grace is a <hi type="italic">word which he hath commanded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.8">Ps. cv. 8</reference>. He <hi type="italic">made an end of commanding,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">etelesendiatasson</hi></hi>. Note, The instructions Christ gives are full instructions. He goes through with his work. <div eID="gen22056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22057" type="x-p"/> 2. When Christ had said what he had to say to his disciples, he <hi type="italic">departed thence.</hi> It should seem they were very loth to leave their Master, till <hi type="italic">he departed</hi> and separated himself from them; as the nurse withdraws the hand, that the child may learn to go by itself. Christ would now teach them how to live, and how to work, without his bodily presence. It was <hi type="italic">expedient for them,</hi> that Christ should thus go away for awhile, that they might be prepared for his long departure, and that, by the help of the Spirit, their own hands might be <hi type="italic">sufficient for them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.7">Deut. xxxiii. 7</reference>), and they might not be always children. We have little account of what they did now pursuant to their commission. They went abroad, no doubt; probably into Judea (for in Galilee the gospel had been mostly preached hitherto), publishing the doctrine of Christ, and working miracles in his name: but still in a more immediate dependence upon him, and not being long from him; and thus they were trained up, by degrees, for their great work. <div eID="gen22057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22058" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ departed, <hi type="italic">to teach and preach</hi> in the cities whither he sent his disciples before him to <hi type="italic">work miracles</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.1-Matt.10.8">ch. x. 1-8</reference>), and so to raise people's expectations, and to make way for his entertainment. Thus was the <hi type="italic">way of the Lord prepared;</hi> John prepared it by bringing people to <hi type="italic">repentance,</hi> but he did <hi type="italic">no miracles.</hi> The disciples go further, they <hi type="italic">work miracles</hi> for confirmation. Note, Repentance and faith prepare people for the blessings of the kingdom of heaven, which Christ gives. Observe, When Christ empowered them to <hi type="italic">work miracles,</hi> he employed himself in <hi type="italic">teaching</hi> and <hi type="italic">preaching,</hi> as if that were the more honourable of the two. That was but in order to do this. Healing the sick was the <hi type="italic">saving of bodies,</hi> but preaching the gospel was to the <hi type="italic">saving of souls.</hi> Christ had directed his disciples to preach (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.7">ch. x. 7</reference>), yet he did not leave off preaching himself. He set them to work, not for his own ease, but for the ease of the country, and was not the less busy for employing them. How unlike are they to Christ, who yoke others only that they may themselves be idle! Note, the increase and multitude of labourers in the Lord's work should be made not an excuse for our negligence, but an encouragement to our diligence. The more busy others are, the more busy we should be, and all little enough, so much work is there to be done. Observe, he went to preach <hi type="italic">in their cities,</hi> which were populous places; he cast the net of the gospel where there were most fish to be enclosed. Wisdom cries in <hi type="italic">the cities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.21">Prov. i. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">at the entry of the city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.3">Prov. viii. 3</reference>), in <hi type="italic">the cities of the Jews,</hi> even of them who made light of him, who notwithstanding had the first offer. <div eID="gen22058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22059" type="x-p"/> What he preached we are not told, but it was probably to the same purpose with his sermon on the mount. But here is next recorded a message which John Baptist sent to Christ, and his return to it, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.2-Matt.11.6">v. 2-6</reference>. We heard before that Jesus heard of John's sufferings, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.12">ch. iv. 12</reference>. Now we are told that John, in prison, hears of Christ's doings. He <hi type="italic">heard in the prison the works of Christ;</hi> and no doubt he was glad to hear of them, for he was a true friend of the Bridegroom, <reference osisRef="John.3.29">John iii. 29</reference>. Note, When one useful instrument is laid aside, God knows how to raise up many others in the stead of it. The work went on, though John was in prison, and it added no affliction, but a great deal of consolation, to his bonds. Nothing more comfortable to God's people in distress, than to <hi type="italic">hear of the works of Christ;</hi> especially to experience them in their own souls. This turns a prison into a palace. Some way or other Christ will convey the notices of his love to those that are in trouble for conscience sake. John could not see the works of Christ, but he heard of them with pleasure. And blessed are they who <hi type="italic">have not seen,</hi> but only heard, and yet <hi type="italic">have believed.</hi> <div eID="gen22059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22060" type="x-p"/> Now John Baptist, hearing of Christ's works, sent two of his disciples to him; and what passed between them and him we have here an account of. Here is, <div eID="gen22060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22061" type="x-p"/> I. The question they had to propose to him: <hi type="italic">Art thou he that should come, or do we look for another?</hi> This was a serious and important question; <hi type="italic">Art thou the Messiah promised, or not? Art thou the Christ? Tell us.</hi> 1. It is taken for granted that the Messiah should come. It was one of the names by which he was known to the Old-Testament saints, <hi type="italic">he that cometh or shall come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.26">Ps. cxviii. 26</reference>. He is now come, but there is another coming of his which we still expect. 2. They intimate, that if this be not <hi type="italic">he,</hi> they would <hi type="italic">look for another.</hi> Note, We must not be weary of looking for him that is to come, nor ever say, we will not more expect him till we come to enjoy him. Though he tarry, wait for him, for he that shall come will come, though not in our time. 3. They intimate likewise, that if they be convinced that this is he, they will not be sceptics, they will be satisfied, and will look <hi type="italic">for no other.</hi> 4. They therefore ask, <hi type="italic">Art thou he?</hi> John had said for his part, <hi type="italic">I am not the Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.20">John i. 20</reference>. Now, (1.) Some think that John sent this question for his own satisfaction. It is true he had borne a noble testimony to Christ; he had declared him to be the <hi type="italic">Son of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.34">John i. 34</reference>), the Lamb of God (<reference osisRef="John.1.29">v. 29</reference>), and he that <hi type="italic">should baptize with the Holy Ghost</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.33">v. 33</reference>), and <hi type="italic">sent of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">John iii. 34</reference>), which were great things. But he desired to be further and more fully assured, that he was the Messiah that had been so long promised and expected. Note, In matters relating to Christ and our salvation by him, it is good to be sure. Christ appeared not in that external pomp and power in which it was expected he should appear; his own disciples stumbled at this, and perhaps John did so; Christ saw something of this at the bottom of this enquiry, when he said, <hi type="italic">blessed is he who shall not be offended in me.</hi> Note, It is hard, even for good men, to bear up against vulgar errors. (2.) John's doubt might arise from his own present circumstances. He was a prisoner, and might be tempted to think, if Jesus be indeed the Messiah, whence is it that I, his friend and forerunner, am brought into this trouble, and am left to be so long in it, and he never looks after me, never visits me, nor sends to me, enquires not after me, does nothing either to sweeten my imprisonment or hasten my enlargement? Doubtless there was a good reason why our Lord Jesus did not go to John in prison, lest there should seem to have been a compact between them: but John construed it into a neglect, and it was perhaps a shock to his faith in Christ. Note, [1.] Where there is true faith, yet there may be a mixture of unbelief. The best are not always alike strong. [2.] Troubles for Christ, especially when they continue long unrelieved, are such trials of faith as sometimes prove too hard to be borne up against. [3.] The remaining unbelief of good men may sometimes, in an hour of temptation, strike at the root, and call in question the most fundamental truths which were thought to be well settled. <hi type="italic">Will the Lord cast off for ever?</hi> But we will hope that John's faith did not fail in this matter, only he desired to have it strengthened and confirmed. Note, The best saints have need of the best helps they can get for the strengthening of their faith, and the arming of themselves against temptations to infidelity. Abraham believed, and yet desired a sign (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.6">Gen. xv. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.8">8</reference>), so did Gideon, <reference osisRef="Judg.6.36">Judg. vi. 36</reference>. But, (3.) Others think that John sent his disciples to Christ with this question, not so much for his own satisfaction as for theirs. Observe, Though he was a prisoner they adhered to him, attended on him, and were ready to receive instructions from him; they loved him, and would not leave him. Now, [1.] They were weak in knowledge, and wavering in their faith, and needed instruction and confirmation; and in this matter they were somewhat prejudiced; being jealous <hi type="italic">for their</hi> master, they were jealous <hi type="italic">of our</hi> Master; they were loth to acknowledge Jesus to be the Messiah, because he eclipsed John, and are loth to believe their own master when they think he speaks against himself and them. Good men are apt to have their judgments blessed by their interest. Now John would have their mistakes rectified, and wished them to be as well satisfied as he himself was. Note, The strong ought to consider the infirmities of the weak, and to do what they can to help them: and such as we cannot help ourselves we should send to those that can. <hi type="italic">When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.</hi> [2.] John was all along industrious to turn over his disciples to Christ, as from the grammar-school to the academy. Perhaps he foresaw his death approaching, and therefore would bring his disciples to be better acquainted with Christ, under whose guardianship he must leave them. Note, Ministers' business is to direct every body to Christ. And those who would know the certainty of the doctrine of Christ, must apply themselves to him, who is come to give an understanding. They who would grow in grace must be inquisitive. <div eID="gen22061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22062" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Christ's answer to this question, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.4-Matt.11.6">v. 4-6</reference>. It was not so direct and express, as when he said, <hi type="italic">I that speak unto thee am he;</hi> but it was a real answer, an answer in fact. Christ will have us to spell out the convincing evidences of gospel truths, and to take pains in digging for knowledge. <div eID="gen22062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22063" type="x-p"/> 1. He points them to what they heard and saw, which they must tell John, that he might from thence take occasion the more fully to instruct and convince them out of their own mouths. Go and tell him <hi type="italic">what you hear and see.</hi> Note, Our senses may and ought to be appealed to in those things that are their proper objects. Therefore the popish doctrine of the real presence agrees not with the truth <hi type="italic">as it is in Jesus;</hi> for Christ refers us to the things we <hi type="italic">hear and see. Go and tell John,</hi> <div eID="gen22063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22064" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">What you see</hi> of the <hi type="italic">power of Christ's miracles;</hi> you see how, by the word of Jesus, <hi type="italic">the blind receive their sight,</hi> the <hi type="italic">lame walk,</hi> &c. Christ's miracles were done openly, and in the view of all; for they feared not the strongest and most impartial scrutiny. <hi type="italic">Veritas no quærit angulos—Truth seeks not concealment.</hi> They are to be considered, [1.] As the <hi type="italic">acts of a divine power.</hi> None but the God of nature could thus overrule and outdo the power of nature. It is particularly spoken of as God's prerogative to <hi type="italic">open the eyes of the blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.146.8">Ps. cxlvi. 8</reference>. Miracles are therefore the broad seal of heaven, and the doctrine they are affixed to must be of God, for his power will never contradict his truth; nor can it be imagined that he should set his seal to a lie; however <hi type="italic">lying wonders</hi> may be vouched for in proof of <hi type="italic">false doctrines, true miracles</hi> evince a divine commission; such Christ's were, and they leave no room to doubt that he was sent of God, and that his doctrine was his that <hi type="italic">sent him.</hi> [2.] As the <hi type="italic">accomplishment of a divine prediction.</hi> It was foretold (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5-Isa.35.6">Isa. xxxv. 5, 6</reference>), that our God should come, and that then <hi type="italic">the eyes of the blind should be opened.</hi> Now if the works of Christ agree with the words of the prophet, as it is plain they do, then no doubt but this is our God whom we have waited for, who shall <hi type="italic">come with a recompence;</hi> this is he who is so much wanted. <div eID="gen22064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22065" type="x-p"/> (2.) Tell him <hi type="italic">what you hear</hi> of the <hi type="italic">preaching of his gospel,</hi> which accompanies his miracles. Faith, though confirmed by seeing, comes by hearing. Tell him, [1.] That <hi type="italic">the poor preach the gospel;</hi> so some read it. It proves Christ's divine mission, that those whom he employed in founding his kingdom were poor men, destitute of all secular advantages, who, therefore, could never have carried their point, if they had not been carried on by a divine power. [2.] That <hi type="italic">the poor have the gospel preached to them.</hi> Christ's auditory is made up of such as the scribes and Pharisees despised, and looked upon with contempt, and the <hi type="italic">rabbies</hi> would not instruct, because they were notable to pay them. The <hi type="italic">Old-Testament</hi> prophets were sent mostly to kings and princes, but Christ preached to the <hi type="italic">congregations of the poor.</hi> It was foretold that the <hi type="italic">poor of the flock</hi> should <hi type="italic">wait upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.11.11">Zech. xi. 11</reference>. Note, Christ's gracious condescensions and compassions to <hi type="italic">the poor,</hi> are an evidence that it was he that should bring to the world the tender mercies of our God. It was foretold that the <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi> should be the <hi type="italic">poor man's King,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Ps. lxxii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.4">4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.12">12,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.13">13</reference>. Or we may understand it, not so much of the <hi type="italic">poor of the world,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">poor in spirit,</hi> and so that scripture is fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>, <hi type="italic">He hath anointed me to preach glad tidings to the meek.</hi> Note, It is a proof of Christ's divine mission that his doctrine is gospel indeed; good news to those who are truly humbled in sorrow for their sins, and truly humble in the denial of self; to them it is accommodated, for whom God always declared he had mercy in store. [3.] That the <hi type="italic">poor receive the gospel,</hi> and are wrought upon by it, they are evangelized, they receive and entertain the gospel, are leavened by it, and delivered into it as into a mould. Note, The wonderful efficacy of the gospel is a proof of its divine original. The poor are <hi type="italic">wrought upon</hi> by it. The prophets complained of <hi type="italic">the poor,</hi> that they <hi type="italic">knew not the way of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.5.4">Jer. v. 4</reference>. They could do no good upon them; but the gospel of Christ made its way into their untutored minds. <div eID="gen22065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22066" type="x-p"/> 2. He pronounces a <hi type="italic">blessing</hi> on those that <hi type="italic">were not offended in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.6">v. 6</reference>. So clear are these evidences of Christ's mission, that they who are not wilfully prejudiced against him, and scandalized in him (so the word is), cannot but receive his doctrine, and so be <hi type="italic">blessed in him.</hi> Note, (1.) There are many things in Christ which they who are ignorant and unthinking are apt to be offended at, some circumstances for the sake of which they reject the substance of his gospel. The meanness of his appearance, his education at Nazareth, the poverty of his life, the despicableness of his followers, the slights which the great men put upon him, the strictness of his doctrine, the contradiction it gives to flesh and blood, and the sufferings that attend the profession of his name; these are things that keep many from him, who otherwise cannot but see much of God in him. Thus he is set <hi type="italic">for the fall of many,</hi> even in Israel (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Luke ii. 34</reference>), a <hi type="italic">Rock of offence,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.8">1 Pet. ii. 8</reference>. (2.) They are happy who get over these offences. <hi type="italic">Blessed are they.</hi> The expression intimates, that it is a difficult thing to conquer these prejudices, and a dangerous thing not to conquer them; but as to those, who, notwithstanding this opposition, to believe in Christ, their faith will be found so much the more, to <hi type="italic">praise, and honour, and glory.</hi>
entries.b3ac5ffb1364b460ecef72a5600994e9517aa286: <div eID="gen22066" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Testimony of John.</title> <div sID="gen22067" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And as they departed, Jesus began to say unto the multitudes concerning John, What went ye out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken with the wind? <hi type="super">8</hi> But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? behold, they that wear soft <hi type="italic">clothing</hi> are in kings' houses. <hi type="super">9</hi> But what went ye out for to see? A prophet? yea, I say unto you, and more than a prophet. <hi type="super">10</hi> For this is <hi type="italic">he,</hi> of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee. <hi type="super">11</hi> Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he. <hi type="super">12</hi> And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffereth violence, and the violent take it by force. <hi type="super">13</hi> For all the prophets and the law prophesied until <reference osisRef="John.14">John. 14</reference> And if ye will receive <hi type="italic">it,</hi> this is Elias, which was for to come. <hi type="super">15</hi> He that hath ears to hear, let him hear. <div eID="gen22067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22068" type="x-p"/> We have here the high encomium which our Lord Jesus gave of John the Baptist; not only to revive his honour, but to revive his work. Some of Christ's disciples might perhaps take occasion from the question John sent, to reflect upon him, as weak and wavering, and inconsistent with himself, to prevent which Christ gives him this character. Note, It is our duty to consult the reputation of our brethren, and not only to remove, but to obviate and prevent, jealousies and ill thoughts of them; and we must take all occasions, especially such as discover any thing of infirmity, to speak well of those who are praiseworthy, and to give them that <hi type="italic">fruit of their hands.</hi> John the Baptist, when he was upon the stage, and Christ in privacy and retirement, bore testimony to Christ; and now that Christ appeared publicly, and John was under a cloud, he bore testimony to John. Note, They who have a confirmed interest themselves, should improve it for the helping of the credit and reputation of others, whose character claims it, but whose temper or present circumstances put them out of the way of it. This is giving honour to whom honour is due. John had abased himself to honour Christ (<reference osisRef="John.3.20">John iii. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.30">30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.11">ch. iii. 11</reference>), had made himself nothing, that Christ might be All, and now Christ dignifies him with this character. Note, They who humble themselves shall be exalted, and those that honour Christ he will honour; those that confess him before men, he will confess, and sometimes <hi type="italic">before men</hi> too, even in this world. John had now <hi type="italic">finished his testimony,</hi> and now Christ commends him. Note, Christ reserves honour for his servants when they <hi type="italic">have done their work,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.26">John xii. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen22068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22069" type="x-p"/> Now concerning this commendation of John, observe, <div eID="gen22069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22070" type="x-p"/> I. That Christ spoke thus honourably of John, not in the hearing of John's disciples, but <hi type="italic">as they departed,</hi> just after they were gone, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.24">Luke vii. 24</reference>. He would not so much as seem to flatter John, nor have these praises of him reported to him. Note, Though we must be forward to give to all their due praise for their encouragement, yet we must avoid every thing that looks like flattery, or may be in danger of puffing them up. They who in other things are mortified to the world, yet cannot well bear their own praise. Pride is a corrupt humour, which we must not feed either in others or in ourselves. <div eID="gen22070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22071" type="x-p"/> II. That what Christ said concerning John, was intended not only for his praise, but for the people's profit, to revive the remembrance of John's ministry, which had been well attended, but which was now (as other such things used to be) strangely forgotten: they did for a season, and but <hi type="italic">for a season, rejoice in his light,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.5.35">John v. 35</reference>. "Now, consider, <hi type="italic">what went ye out into the wilderness to see?</hi> Put this question to yourselves." 1. John preached <hi type="italic">in the wilderness,</hi> and thither people flocked in crowds to him, though in a <hi type="italic">remote</hi> place, and an <hi type="italic">inconvenient</hi> one. If teachers be removed into corners, it is better to go after them than to be without them. Now if his preaching was worth taking so much pains to hear it, surely it was worth taking some care to recollect it. The greater the difficulties we have broken through to hear the word, the more we are concerned to profit by it. 2. They went out to him to see him; rather to feed their eyes with the unusual appearance of his person, than to feed their souls with his wholesome instructions; rather for curiosity than for conscience. Note, Many that attend on the word come rather to see and be seen, than to learn and be taught, to have something to talk of, than to be made wise to salvation. Christ puts it to them, <hi type="italic">what went ye out to see?</hi> Note, They who attend on the word will be called to an account, what their intentions and what their improvements were. We think when the sermon is done, the care is over; no, then the greatest of the care begins. It will shortly be asked, "What business had you such a time at such an ordinance? <hi type="italic">What brought you thither?</hi> Was it custom or company, or was it a desire to honour God and get good? <hi type="italic">What have you brought thence?</hi> What knowledge, and grace, and comfort? <hi type="italic">What went you to see?</hi>" Note, When we go to read and hear the word, we should see that we aim right in what we do. <div eID="gen22071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22072" type="x-p"/> III. Let us see what the commendation of John was. They know not what answer to make to Christ's question; well, says Christ, "I will tell you what a man John the Baptist was." <div eID="gen22072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22073" type="x-p"/> 1. "He was a firm, resolute man, and not <hi type="italic">a reed shaken with the wind; you</hi> have been so in your thoughts of him, but <hi type="italic">he</hi> was not so. He was not wavering in his principles, nor uneven in his conversation; but was remarkable for his steadiness and constant consistency with himself." They who are <hi type="italic">weak</hi> as reeds will be <hi type="italic">shaken</hi> as reeds; but John was <hi type="italic">strong in spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Eph. iv. 14</reference>. When the wind of popular applause on the one hand blew fresh and fair, when the storm of Herod's rage on the other hand grew fierce and blustering, John was still the same, the same in all weathers. The testimony he had borne to Christ was not the testimony of <hi type="italic">a reed,</hi> of a man who was of one mind to-day, and of another to-morrow; it was not a weather-cock testimony; no, his constancy in it is intimated (<reference osisRef="John.1.20">John i. 20</reference>); he <hi type="italic">confessed and denied not, but confessed,</hi> and stood to it afterwards, <reference osisRef="John.3.28">John iii. 28</reference>. And therefore this question sent by his disciples was not to be construed into any suspicion of the truth of what he had formerly said: therefore the people flocked to him, because he was not as a reed. Note, There is nothing lost in the long run by an unshaken resolution to go on with our work, neither courting the smiles, nor fearing the frowns of men. <div eID="gen22073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22074" type="x-p"/> 2. He was a <hi type="italic">self-denying</hi> man, and <hi type="italic">mortified</hi> to this world. "Was he a man <hi type="italic">clothed in soft raiment?</hi> If so, you would not have gone <hi type="italic">into the wilderness</hi> to see him, but to the <hi type="italic">court.</hi> You went to see one that had <hi type="italic">his raiment of camel's hair,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">leathern girdle about his loins;</hi> his mien and habit showed that he was dead to all the pomps of the world and the pleasures of sense; his clothing agreed with the <hi type="italic">wilderness</hi> he lived in, and the doctrine he preached there, that of repentance. Now you cannot think that he who was such a stranger to the pleasures of a court, should be brought to change his mind by the terrors of a prison, and now to question whether Jesus be the Messiah or not!" Note, they who have lived a life of mortification, are least likely to be driven off from their religion by persecution. He was not a man clothed in <hi type="italic">soft raiment;</hi> such <hi type="italic">there are,</hi> but they are <hi type="italic">in kings' houses.</hi> Note, It becomes people in all their appearances to be consistent with their character and their situation. They who are preachers must not affect to look like courtiers; nor must they whose lot is cast in common dwellings, be ambitious of the soft clothing which they wear who are in kings' houses. Prudence teaches us to be <hi type="italic">of a piece.</hi> John appeared rough and unpleasant, yet they flocked after him. Note, The remembrance of our former zeal in attending on the word of God, should quicken us to, and in, our present work: let it not be said that we have done and suffered so many things <hi type="italic">in vain,</hi> have <hi type="italic">run in vain</hi> and <hi type="italic">laboured in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen22074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22075" type="x-p"/> 3. His greatest commendation of all was his office and ministry, which was more his honour than any personal endowments or qualifications could be; and therefore this is most enlarged upon in a full encomium. <div eID="gen22075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22076" type="x-p"/> (1.) He was <hi type="italic">a prophet,</hi> yea, and <hi type="italic">more than a prophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.9">v. 9</reference>); so he said of him who was the great Prophet, to whom all the prophets bear witness. John said of himself, he was not <hi type="italic">that prophet,</hi> that great prophet, the Messiah himself; and now Christ (a very competent Judge) says of him, that he was <hi type="italic">more than a prophet.</hi> He owned himself inferior to Christ, and Christ owned him superior to all other prophets. Observe, The forerunner of Christ was not a king, but a prophet, lest it should seem that the kingdom of the Messiah had been laid in earthly power; but his immediate forerunner was, as such, a <hi type="italic">transcendent</hi> prophet, more than an <hi type="italic">Old-Testament prophet;</hi> they all <hi type="italic">did virtuously,</hi> but John excelled them all; they <hi type="italic">saw Christ's day</hi> at a distance, and their vision was yet for a great while to come; but John saw the day dawn, he saw the sun rise, and told the people of the Messiah, as one that stood among them. They spake of Christ, but he pointed to him; they said, <hi type="italic">A virgin shall conceive:</hi> he said, <hi type="italic">Behold the Lamb of God!</hi> <div eID="gen22076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22077" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was the same that was predicted to be Christ's forerunner (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.10">v. 10</reference>); <hi type="italic">This is he of whom it is written.</hi> He was prophesied of by the other prophets, and therefore was greater than they. Malachi prophesied concerning John, <hi type="italic">Behold, I send my messenger before thy face.</hi> Herein some of Christ's honour was put upon him, that the <hi type="italic">Old-Testament</hi> prophets spake and wrote of him; and this honour have all the saints, that their <hi type="italic">names</hi> are <hi type="italic">written in the Lamb's book of life.</hi> It was great preferment to John above all the prophets, that he was Christ's harbinger. He was a <hi type="italic">messenger</hi> sent on a great errand; a messenger, <hi type="italic">one among a thousand,</hi> deriving his honour from his whose messenger he was: he is <hi type="italic">my messenger</hi> sent <hi type="italic">of God.</hi> His business was to <hi type="italic">prepare Christ's way,</hi> to dispose people to receive the Saviour, by discovering to them their sin and misery, and their need of a Saviour. This he had said of himself (<reference osisRef="John.1.23">John i. 23</reference>) and now Christ said it of him; intending hereby not only to put an honour upon John's ministry, but to revive people's regard to it, as making way for the Messiah. Note, Much of the beauty of God's dispensations lies in their mutual connection and coherence, and the reference they have one to another. That which advanced John above the <hi type="italic">Old-Testament</hi> prophets was, that he went immediately before Christ. Note, The nearer any are to Christ, the more truly honourable they are. <div eID="gen22077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22078" type="x-p"/> (3.) There <hi type="italic">was not a greater born of women</hi> than John the Baptist, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.11">v. 11</reference>. Christ knew how to value persons according to the degrees of their worth, and he prefers John before all that went before him, before all that were <hi type="italic">born of women</hi> by ordinary generation. Of all that God had raised up and called to any service in his church, John is the most eminent, even beyond Moses himself; for he began to preach the gospel doctrine of remission of sins to those who are truly penitent; and he had more signal revelations from heaven than any of them had; for he <hi type="italic">saw heaven opened,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Holy Ghost descend.</hi> He also had great success in his ministry; almost the whole nation flocked to him: none rose on so great a design, or came on so noble an errand, as John did, or had such claims to a welcome reception. Many had been born of women that made a great figure in the world, but Christ prefers John before them. Note, Greatness is not to be measured by appearances and outward splendour, but they are the greatest men who are the greatest saints, and the greatest blessings, who are, as John was, <hi type="italic">great in the sight of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.15">Luke i. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen22078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22079" type="x-p"/> Yet this high encomium of John has a surprising limitation, <hi type="italic">notwithstanding, he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.</hi> [1.] In the kingdom of <hi type="italic">glory.</hi> John was a <hi type="italic">great</hi> and <hi type="italic">good</hi> man, but he was yet in a state of infirmity and imperfection, and therefore came short of glorified saints, and the <hi type="italic">spirits of just men made perfect.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There are degrees of glory in heaven, some that are less than others there; though every vessel is alike full, all are not alike large and capacious. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The least saint in heaven is <hi type="italic">greater,</hi> and knows more, and loves more, and does more in praising God, and receives more from him, than the greatest in this world. The saints on earth are excellent ones (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Ps. xvi. 3</reference>), but those in heaven are much more excellent; the best in this world are <hi type="italic">lower than the angels</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Ps. viii. 5</reference>), the least there are <hi type="italic">equal with the angels,</hi> which should make us long for that blessed state, where the <hi type="italic">weak shall be as David,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.12.8">Zech. xii. 8</reference>. [2.] By the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven</hi> here, is rather to be understood the <hi type="italic">kingdom of grace,</hi> the gospel dispensation in the perfection of its power and purity; and ho mikroteros—<hi type="italic">he that is less</hi> in that is <hi type="italic">greater than John.</hi> Some understand it of Christ himself, who was younger than John, and, in the opinion of some, less than John, who always spoke diminishingly of himself; <hi type="italic">I am a worm, and no man,</hi> yet greater than John; so it agrees with what John the Baptist said (<reference osisRef="John.1.15">John i. 15</reference>), <hi type="italic">He that cometh after me is preferred before me.</hi> But it is rather to be understood of the apostles and ministers of the <hi type="italic">New Testament,</hi> the evangelical prophets; and the comparison between them and John is not with respect to their personal sanctity, but to their office; John preached Christ coming, but they preached Christ not only come, but <hi type="italic">crucified</hi> and <hi type="italic">glorified.</hi> John came to the dawning of the gospel-day, and therein excelled the foregoing prophets, but he was taken off before the noon of that day, before the rending of the veil, before Christ's death and resurrection, and the pouring out of the Spirit; so that the least of the apostles and evangelists, having greater discoveries made to them, and being employed in a greater embassy, is <hi type="italic">greater than John.</hi> John did no miracles; the apostles wrought many. The ground of this preference is laid in the preference of the <hi type="italic">New</hi>-Testament dispensation to that of the <hi type="italic">Old</hi> Testament. Ministers of the New Testament therefore excel, because their ministration does so, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.6">2 Cor. iii. 6</reference>, &c. John was a <hi type="italic">maximum quod sic—the greatest of his order;</hi> he went to the utmost that the dispensation he was under would allow; but <hi type="italic">minimum maximi est majus maximo minimi—the least of the highest order is superior to the first of the lowest;</hi> a dwarf upon a mountain sees further than a giant in the valley. Note, All the true greatness of men is derived from, and denominated by, the gracious manifestation of Christ to them. The best men are no better than he is pleased to make them. What reason have we to be thankful that our lot is cast in the days of the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven,</hi> under such advantages of light and love! And the greater the advantages, the greater will the account be, if we <hi type="italic">receive the grace of God in vain.</hi> <div eID="gen22079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22080" type="x-p"/> (4.) The great commendation of John the Baptist was, that God owned his ministry, and made it wonderfully successful for the breaking of the ice, and the preparing of people for the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven. From the days of</hi> the first appearing of <hi type="italic">John the Baptist,</hi> until now (which was not much above two years), a great deal of good was done; so quick was the motion when it came near to Christ the Centre; <hi type="italic">The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">biazetai</hi></hi>-<hi type="italic">vim patitur,</hi> like the violence of an army taking a city by storm, or of a crowd bursting into a house, so the <hi type="italic">violent take it by force.</hi> The meaning of this we have in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luke xvi. 16</reference>. Since that time <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is preached, and every man presseth into it.</hi> Multitudes are wrought upon by the ministry of John, and become his disciples. And it is <div eID="gen22080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22081" type="x-p"/> [1.] An <hi type="italic">improbable</hi> multitude. Those strove for a place in this kingdom, that one would think had no right nor title to it, and so seemed to be intruders, and to make a <hi type="italic">tortuous</hi> entry, as our law calls it, a wrongful and forcible one. When the <hi type="italic">children of the kingdom</hi> are excluded out of it, and many come into it <hi type="italic">from the east and the west,</hi> then it <hi type="italic">suffers violence.</hi> Compare this with <reference osisRef="Matt.21.31-Matt.21.32">ch. xxi. 31, 32</reference>. The publicans and harlots believed John, whom the scribes and Pharisees rejected, and so went into the kingdom of God before them, <hi type="italic">took it over their heads,</hi> while they trifled. Note, It is no breach of good manners to go to heaven before our betters: and it is a great commendation of the gospel from the days of its infancy, that it has brought many to holiness that were very unlikely. <div eID="gen22081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22082" type="x-p"/> [2.] An <hi type="italic">importunate</hi> multitude. This violence denotes a strength, and vigour, and earnestness of desire and endeavour, in those who followed John's ministry, else they would not have come so far to attend upon it. It shows us also, what fervency and zeal are required of all those who design to make heaven of their religion. Note, They who would <hi type="italic">enter into the kingdom of heaven</hi> must <hi type="italic">strive to enter;</hi> that kingdom suffers a holy violence; self must be denied, the bent and bias, the frame and temper, of the mind must be altered; there are hard sufferings to be undergone, a force to be put upon the corrupt nature; we must run, and wrestle, and fight, and be <hi type="italic">in an agony,</hi> and all little enough to win such a prize, and to get over such opposition from without and from within. <hi type="italic">The violent take it by force.</hi> They who will have an interest in the great salvation are carried out towards it with a strong desire, will have it <hi type="italic">upon any terms,</hi> and not think them hard, nor quit their hold without a blessing, <reference osisRef="Gen.32.26">Gen. xxxii. 26</reference>. They who will make their calling and election sure must give diligence. The kingdom of heaven was never intended to indulge the ease of triflers, but to be the rest of them that labour. It is a blessed sight; Oh that we could see a greater number, not with an <hi type="italic">angry</hi> contention thrusting others out of the kingdom of heaven, but with a <hi type="italic">holy</hi> contention thrusting themselves into it! <div eID="gen22082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22083" type="x-p"/> (5.) The ministry of John was the <hi type="italic">beginning of the gospel,</hi> as it is reckoned, <reference osisRef="Mark.1.1">Mark i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.22">Acts i. 22</reference>. This is shown here in two things: <div eID="gen22083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22084" type="x-p"/> [1.] In John the Old Testament dispensation began to die, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.13">v. 13</reference>. So long that ministration continued in full force and virtue, but then it began to decline. Though the obligation of the law of Moses was not removed till Christ's death, yet the discoveries of the Old Testament began to be superseded by the more clear manifestation of the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven</hi> as <hi type="italic">at hand.</hi> Because the <hi type="italic">light of the gospel</hi> (as that of nature) was to precede and make way for its <hi type="italic">law,</hi> therefore the prophecies of the Old Testament came to an end (<hi type="italic">finis perficiens,</hi> not <hi type="italic">interficiens—an end of completion, not of duration</hi>), before the precepts of it; so that when Christ says, <hi type="italic">all the prophets and the law prophesied until John,</hi> he shows us, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> How the light of the Old Testament was set up; it was set up in <hi type="italic">the law and the prophets,</hi> who spoke, though darkly, of Christ and his kingdom. Observe, The <hi type="italic">law</hi> is said to prophesy, as well as the <hi type="italic">prophets,</hi> concerning him that was to come. Christ <hi type="italic">began at Moses</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.27">Luke xxiv. 27</reference>); Christ was foretold by the dumb signs of the Mosaic work, as well as by the more articulate voices of the prophets, and was exhibited, not only in the verbal predictions, but in the personal and real types. Blessed be God that we have both the New-Testament doctrine to explain the Old-Testament prophecies, and the Old-Testament prophecies to confirm and illustrate the New-Testament doctrine (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.1">Heb. i. 1</reference>); like the two cherubim, they look at each other. The law was given by Moses long ago, and there had been no prophets for three hundred years before John, and yet they are both said to <hi type="italic">prophecy until John,</hi> because the law was still observed, and Moses and the prophets still read. Note, The scripture is teaching to this day, though the penmen of it are gone. Moses and the prophets are dead; the apostles and evangelists are dead (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.5">Zech. i. 5</reference>), but the <hi type="italic">word of the Lord endures for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.25">1 Pet. i. 25</reference>); the <hi type="italic">scripture</hi> is <hi type="italic">speaking expressly,</hi> though the writers are silent in the dust. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> How this light was <hi type="italic">laid aside:</hi> when he says, they <hi type="italic">prophesied until John,</hi> he intimates, that their glory was eclipsed by the glory which excelled; their predictions superseded by John's testimony, <hi type="italic">Behold the Lamb of God!</hi> Even before the sun rises, the morning light makes candles to shine dim. Their prophecies of a Christ to come became out of date, when John said, <hi type="italic">He is come.</hi> <div eID="gen22084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22085" type="x-p"/> [2.] In him the New-Testament day began to dawn; for (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.14">v. 14</reference>) <hi type="italic">This is Elias, that was for to come.</hi> John was as the loop that coupled the two Testaments; as Noah was <hi type="italic">Fibula utriusque mundi—the link connecting both worlds,</hi> so was he <hi type="italic">utriusque Testamenti—the link connecting both Testaments.</hi> The concluding prophecy of the Old Testament was, <hi type="italic">Behold, I will send you Elijah,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.4.5-Mal.4.6">Mal. iv. 5, 6</reference>. Those words prophesied until John, and then, being turned into a history, they ceased to prophecy. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ speaks of it as a great truth, that John the Baptist is the Elias of the New Testament; not Elias <hi type="italic">in propria persona—in his own person,</hi> as the carnal Jews expected; he denied that (<reference osisRef="John.1.21">John i. 21</reference>), but one that should come in the spirit and power of Elias (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Luke i. 17</reference>), like him in temper and conversation, that should press repentance with terrors, and especially as it is in the prophecy, that should <hi type="italic">turn the hearts of the fathers to the children. Secondly,</hi> He speaks of it as a truth, which would not be easily apprehended by those whose expectations fastened upon the temporal kingdom of the Messiah, and introductions to it agreeable. Christ suspects the welcome of it, <hi type="italic">if ye will receive it.</hi> Not but that it was true, whether they would receive it or not, but he upbraids them with their prejudices, that they were backward to receive the greatest truths that were opposed to their sentiments, though never so favourable to their interests. Or, "If <hi type="italic">you will receive him,</hi> or if you will receive the ministry of John as that of the promised Elias, he will be an Elias to you, to turn you and prepare you for the Lord," Note, Gospel truths are as they are received, a savour of life or death. Christ is a Saviour, and John an Elias, to those who will receive the truth concerning them. <div eID="gen22085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22086" type="x-p"/> Lastly, Our Lord Jesus closes this discourse with a solemn demand of attention (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that hath ears to hear, let him hear;</hi> which intimates, that those things were dark and hard to be understood, and therefore needed attention, but of great concern and consequence, and therefore well deserved it. "Let all people take notice of this, if John be the Elias prophesied of, then certainly here is a great revolution on foot, the Messiah's kingdom is at the door, and the world will shortly be surprised into a happy change. These are things which require your serious consideration, and therefore you are all concerned to hearken to what I say." Note, The things of God are of great and common concern: every one that has <hi type="italic">ears to hear</hi> any thing, is concerned to hear this. It intimates, that God requires no more from us but the right use and improvement of the faculties he has already given us. He requires those to hear that have ears, those to use their reason that have reason. Therefore people are ignorant, not because they want power, but because they want will; therefore they do not hear, because, like the deaf adder, they <hi type="italic">stop their ears.</hi>
entries.bf690ea261ec030b428e38cc376d63631444b31c: <div eID="gen22086" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Reproaches Chorazin, &c..</title> <div sID="gen22087" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> But whereunto shall I liken this generation? It is like unto children sitting in the markets, and calling unto their fellows, <hi type="super">17</hi> And saying, We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced; we have mourned unto you, and ye have not lamented. <hi type="super">18</hi> For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, He hath a devil. <hi type="super">19</hi> The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not: 21 Woe unto thee, Chorazin! woe unto thee, Bethsaida! for if the mighty works, which were done in you, had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. 22 But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you. <hi type="super">23</hi> And thou, Capernaum, which art exalted unto heaven, shalt be brought down to hell: for if the mighty works, which have been done in thee, had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. <hi type="super">24</hi> But I say unto you, That it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee. <div eID="gen22087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22088" type="x-p"/> Christ was going on in the praise of John the Baptist and his ministry, but here stops on a sudden, and turns that to the reproach of those who enjoyed both that, and the ministry of Christ and his apostles too, in vain. As to that generation, we may observe to whom he <hi type="italic">compares them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.16-Matt.11.19">v. 16-19</reference>), and as to the particular places he instances in, we may observe with whom he <hi type="italic">compares them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.20-Matt.11.24">v. 20-24</reference>. <div eID="gen22088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22089" type="x-p"/> I. As to that <hi type="italic">generation,</hi> the body of the Jewish people at that time. There were many indeed that pressed into the kingdom of heaven; but the generality continued in unbelief and obstinacy. John was a great and good man, but the generation in which his lot was cast was as barren and unprofitable as could be, and unworthy of him. Note, The badness of the places where good ministers live serves for a foil to their beauty. It was Noah's praise that he was <hi type="italic">righteous in his generation.</hi> Having commended John, he condemns those who had him among them, and did not profit by his ministry. Note, The more praise-worthy the people are, if they slight him, and so it will be found in the day of account. <div eID="gen22089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22090" type="x-p"/> This our Lord Jesus here sets forth in a parable, yet speaks as if he were at a loss to find out a similitude proper to represent this, <hi type="italic">Whereunto shall I liken this generation?</hi> Note, There is not a greater absurdity than that which they are guilty of who have good preaching among them, and are never the better for it. It is hard to say <hi type="italic">what they are like.</hi> The similitude is taken from some common custom among the Jewish children at their play, who, as is usual with children, imitated the fashions of grown people at their marriages and funerals, <hi type="italic">rejoicing and lamenting;</hi> but being all a jest, it made no impression; no more did the ministry either of John the Baptist or of Christ upon that generation. He especially reflects on the scribes and Pharisees, who had a proud conceit of themselves; therefore to humble them he compares them to children, and their behaviour to children's play. <div eID="gen22090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22091" type="x-p"/> The parable will be best explained by opening it and the illustration of it together in these five observations. <div eID="gen22091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22092" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The God of heaven uses a variety of proper means and methods for the conversion and salvation of poor souls; he would <hi type="italic">have all men to be saved,</hi> and therefore leaves no stone unturned in order to it. The great thing he aims at, is the <hi type="italic">melting</hi> of our <hi type="italic">wills</hi> into a compliance with the will of God, and in order to this the affecting of us with the discoveries he has made of himself. Having various affections to be wrought upon, he uses various ways of working upon them, which though differing one from another, all tend to the same thing, and God is in them all carrying on the same design. In the parable, this is called his <hi type="italic">piping</hi> to us, and his <hi type="italic">mourning</hi> to us; he hath <hi type="italic">piped to us</hi> in the precious promises of the gospel, proper to work upon hope, and mourned to us in the dreadful threatenings of the law, proper to work upon fear, that he might frighten us out of our sins and allure us to himself. He had <hi type="italic">piped to us</hi> in gracious and merciful providences, <hi type="italic">mourned to us</hi> in calamitous, afflicting providences, and has set the one over against the other. He has taught his ministers to <hi type="italic">change their voice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.20">Gal. iv. 20</reference>); sometimes to speak in thunder from <hi type="italic">mount Sinai,</hi> sometimes in a still small voice from <hi type="italic">mount Sion.</hi> <div eID="gen22092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22093" type="x-p"/> In the explanation of the parable is set forth the different temper of John's ministry and of Christ's, who were the two great lights of that generation. <div eID="gen22093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22094" type="x-p"/> (1.) On the one hand, John came <hi type="italic">mourning to them, neither eating nor drinking;</hi> not conversing familiarly with people, nor ordinarily eating in company, but alone, in his cell in the wilderness, where <hi type="italic">his meat was locusts and wild honey.</hi> Now this, one would think, should work upon them; for such an austere, mortified life as this, was very agreeable to the doctrine he preached: and that minister is most likely to do good, whose conversation is according to his doctrine; and yet the preaching even of such a minister is not always effectual. <div eID="gen22094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22095" type="x-p"/> (2.) On the other hand, <hi type="italic">the Son of man came eating and drinking,</hi> and so he <hi type="italic">piped unto them.</hi> Christ conversed familiarly with all sorts of people, not affecting any peculiar strictness or austerity; he was affable and easy of access, not shy of any company, was often at feasts, both with Pharisees and publicans, to try if this would win upon those who were not wrought upon by John's reservedness: those who were not awed by John's frowns, would be allured by Christ's smiles; from whom St. Paul learned to be come <hi type="italic">all things to all men,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.22">1 Cor. ix. 22</reference>. Now our Lord Jesus, by his freedom, did not at all condemn John, any more than John did condemn him, though their deportment was so very different. Note, Though we are never so clear in the goodness of our own practice, yet we must not judge of others by it. There may be a <hi type="italic">great diversity of operations,</hi> where <hi type="italic">it is the same God that worketh all in all</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">1 Cor. xii. 6</reference>), and this <hi type="italic">various manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.7">v. 7</reference>. Observe especially, that God's ministers are variously gifted: the ability and genius of some lie one way, of others, another way: some are Boanerges—<hi type="italic">sons of thunder;</hi> others, Barnabeses—<hi type="italic">sons of consolation;</hi> yet <hi type="italic">all these worketh that one and the self-same Spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.11">1 Cor. xii. 11</reference>), and therefore we ought not to condemn either, but to praise both, and praise God for both, who thus tries various ways of dealing with persons of various tempers, that sinners may be either made pliable or left inexcusable, so that, whatever the issue is, God will be glorified. <div eID="gen22095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22096" type="x-p"/> Note, 2. The various methods which God takes for the conversion of sinners, are with many fruitless and ineffectual: "<hi type="italic">Ye have not danced, ye have not lamented;</hi> you have not been suitably affected either with the one or with the other." Particular means have, as in medicine, their particular intentions, which must be answered, particular impressions, which must be submitted to, in order to the success of the great and general design; now if people will be neither bound by laws, nor invited by promises, nor frightened by threatenings, will neither be awakened by the <hi type="italic">greatest</hi> things, nor allured by the <hi type="italic">sweetest</hi> things, nor startled by the most <hi type="italic">terrible</hi> things, nor be made sensible by the <hi type="italic">plainest</hi> things; if they will hearken to the voice neither of scripture, nor reason, nor experience, nor providence, nor conscience, nor interest, what more can be done? <hi type="italic">The bellows are burned, the lead is consumed, the founder melteth in vain; reprobate silver shall men call them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.29">Jer. vi. 29</reference>. Ministers' labour is bestowed in vain (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa. xlix. 4</reference>), and, which is a much greater loss, <hi type="italic">the grace of God received in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2 Cor. vi. 1</reference>. Note, It is some comfort to faithful ministers, when they see little success of their labours, that it is no new thing for the best preachers and the best preaching in the world to come short of the desired end. <hi type="italic">Who has believed our report?</hi> If from <hi type="italic">the blood of the slain,</hi> from <hi type="italic">the fat of the mighty,</hi> the bow of those great commanders, Christ and john, returned so often empty (<reference osisRef="2Sam.1.22">2 Sam. i. 22</reference>), no marvel if ours do so, and we prophecy to so little purpose upon dry bones. <div eID="gen22096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22097" type="x-p"/> Note, 3. That commonly those persons who do not profit by the means of grace, are perverse, and reflect upon the ministers by whom they enjoy those means; and because they do not get good themselves, they do all the hurt they can to others, by raising and propagating prejudices against the word, and the faithful preachers of it. Those who will not comply with God, and walk after him, confront him, and walk contrary to him. So <hi type="italic">this generation</hi> did; because they were resolved not to believe Christ and John, and to own them, as they ought to have done, for the best of men, they set themselves to abuse them, and to represent them as the worst. (1.) As for John the Baptist, they say, <hi type="italic">He has a devil.</hi> They imputed his strictness and reservedness to melancholy, and some kind or degree of a possession of Satan. "Why should we heed him? he is a poor hypochondriacal man, full of fancies, and under the power of a crazed imagination." (2.) As for Jesus Christ, they imputed his free and obliging conversation to the more vicious habit of luxury and flesh-pleasing: <hi type="italic">Behold a gluttonous man and a wine-bibber.</hi> No reflection could be more foul and invidious; it is the charge against the rebellious son (<reference osisRef="Deut.21.20">Deut. xxi. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">He is a glutton and a drunkard;</hi> yet none could be more false and unjust; for Christ <hi type="italic">pleased not himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Rom. xv. 3</reference>), nor did ever any man live such a life of self-denial, mortification, and contempt of the world, as Christ lived: he that was <hi type="italic">undefiled, and separate from sinners,</hi> is here represented as in league with them, and polluted by them. Note, The most unspotted innocency, and the most unparalleled excellency, will not always be a fence <hi type="italic">against the reproach of tongues:</hi> nay, a man's best gifts and best actions, which are both well intended and well calculated for edification, may be made the matter of his reproach. The best of our actions may become the worst of our accusations, as David's fasting, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.10">Ps. lxix. 10</reference>. It was true in some sense, that Christ was <hi type="italic">a Friend to publicans and sinners,</hi> the best Friend they ever had, for he <hi type="italic">came into the world to save sinners,</hi> great sinners, even the chief; so he said very feelingly, who had been himself not a <hi type="italic">publican and sinner,</hi> but a Pharisee and sinner; but this is, and will be to eternity, Christ's praise, and they forfeited the benefit of it who thus turned it to his reproach. <div eID="gen22097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22098" type="x-p"/> Note, 4. That the cause of this great unfruitfulness and perverseness of people under the means of grace, is that they are <hi type="italic">like children sitting in the markets;</hi> they are foolish as children, froward as children, mindless and playful as children; would they but <hi type="italic">show themselves men</hi> in understanding, there would be some hopes of them. <hi type="italic">The market-place they sit in</hi> is to some a place of idleness (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.3">ch. xx. 3</reference>); to others a place of worldly business (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.13">James iv. 13</reference>); to all a place of noise or diversion; so that if you ask the reason why people get so little good by the means of grace, you will find it is because they are slothful and trifling, and do not love to take pains; or because their heads, and hands, and hearts are full of the world, the cares of which <hi type="italic">choke the word,</hi> and choke their souls at last ( <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.31">Ezek. xxxiii. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amos viii. 5</reference>); and they study to divert their own thoughts from every thing that is serious. Thus <hi type="italic">in the markets</hi> they are, and there they <hi type="italic">sit;</hi> in these things their hearts rest, and by them they resolve to abide. <div eID="gen22098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22099" type="x-p"/> Note, 5. Though the means of grace be thus slighted and abused by many, by the most, yet there is a remnant that through grace do improve them, and answer the designs of them, to the glory of God, and the good of their own souls. <hi type="italic">But wisdom is justified of her children.</hi> Christ is <hi type="italic">Wisdom;</hi> in him <hi type="italic">are hid treasures of wisdom;</hi> the saints are the <hi type="italic">children God has given</hi> him, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 13</reference>. The gospel is <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">the wisdom from above:</hi> true believers are begotten again by it, and born from above too; they are wise <hi type="italic">children,</hi> wise for themselves, and their true interests; not <hi type="italic">like the foolish children that sat in the markets.</hi> These <hi type="italic">children of wisdom justify wisdom;</hi> they comply with the designs of Christ's grace, answer the intentions of it, and are suitably affected with, and impressed by, the various methods it takes, and so evidence the wisdom of Christ in taking these methods. This is explained, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.29">Luke vii. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">The publicans justified God, being baptized with the baptism of John,</hi> and afterwards embracing the gospel of Christ. Note, The success of the means of grace justifies the wisdom of God in the choice of these means, against those who charge him with folly therein. The cure of every patient, that observes the physician's orders, justifies the wisdom of the physician: and therefore Paul is <hi type="italic">not ashamed of the gospel of Christ,</hi> because, whatever it is to others, <hi type="italic">to them that believe it is the power of God unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Rom. i. 16</reference>. When <hi type="italic">the cross of Christ,</hi> which to others is <hi type="italic">foolishness</hi> and <hi type="italic">a stumbling-block,</hi> is <hi type="italic">to them that are called the wisdom of God and the power of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.23-1Cor.1.24">1 Cor. i. 23, 24</reference>), so that they make the knowledge of that the summit of their ambition (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.2">1 Cor. ii. 2</reference>), and the efficacy of that the crown of their glorying (<reference osisRef="Gal.6.14">Gal. vi. 14</reference>), here is <hi type="italic">wisdom justified of her children. Wisdom's children</hi> are <hi type="italic">wisdom's</hi> witnesses in the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.10">Isa. xliii. 10</reference>), and shall be produced as witnesses in that day, when <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> that is now <hi type="italic">justified</hi> by <hi type="italic">the saints,</hi> shall <hi type="italic">be glorified in the saints,</hi> and <hi type="italic">admired in all them that believe,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2 Thess. i. 10</reference>. If the unbelief of some reproach Christ by giving him the lie, the faith of others shall honour him by setting to its seal that he is true, and that <hi type="italic">he also is wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.25">1 Cor. i. 25</reference>. Whether we do it or not, it will be done; not only God's equity, but his <hi type="italic">wisdom, will be justified when he speaks, when he judges.</hi> <div eID="gen22099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22100" type="x-p"/> Well, this is the account Christ gives of that <hi type="italic">generation,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">generation is not passed away,</hi> but remains in a succession of the like; for as it was then, it has been since and is still; <hi type="italic">some believe the things which are spoken, and some believe not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.28.24">Acts xxviii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen22100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22101" type="x-p"/> II. As to the particular <hi type="italic">places</hi> in which Christ was most conversant. What he said in general of that <hi type="italic">generation,</hi> he applied in particular to those <hi type="italic">places,</hi> to affect them. <hi type="italic">Then began he to upbraid them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.20">v. 20</reference>. He began to preach to them long before (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.17">ch. iv. 17</reference>), but he did not <hi type="italic">begin to upbraid</hi> till now. Note, Rough and unpleasing methods must not be taken, till gentler means have first been used. Christ is not apt <hi type="italic">to upbraid; he gives liberally, and upbraideth not,</hi> till sinners by their obstinacy extort it from him. <hi type="italic">Wisdom</hi> first invites, but when her invitations are slighted, then she <hi type="italic">upbraids,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Prov. i. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.24">24</reference>. Those do not go in Christ's method, who begin with upbraidings. Now observe, <div eID="gen22101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22102" type="x-p"/> 1. The sin charged upon them; not any against the moral law, then an appeal would have lain to the gospel, which would have relieved, but a sin against the gospel, the remedial law, and that is impenitency: this was it he upbraided them with, or reproached them for, as the most shameful, ungrateful thing that could be, that <hi type="italic">they repented not.</hi> Note, Wilful impenitency is the great damning sin of multitudes that enjoy the gospel, and which (more than any other) sinners will be upbraided with to eternity. The great doctrine that both John the Baptist, and Christ, and the apostles preached, was repentance; the great thing designed, both in the <hi type="italic">piping</hi> and in the <hi type="italic">mourning,</hi> was to prevail with people to change their minds and ways, to leave their sins and turn to God; and this they would not be brought to. He does not say, because they <hi type="italic">believed</hi> not (for some kind of faith many of them had) that Christ was a <hi type="italic">Teacher come from God;</hi> but because <hi type="italic">they repented not:</hi> their faith did not prevail to the transforming of their hearts, and the reforming of their lives. Christ reproved them for their other sins, that he might <hi type="italic">lead them to repentance;</hi> but when <hi type="italic">they repented not, He upbraided them</hi> with that, as their refusal <hi type="italic">to be healed: He upbraided them</hi> with it, that they might upbraid themselves, and might at length see the folly of it, as that which alone makes the sad case a desperate one, and the wound incurable. <div eID="gen22102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22103" type="x-p"/> 2. The aggravation of the sin; they were <hi type="italic">the cities in which most of his mighty works were done;</hi> for thereabouts his principal residence had been for some time. Note, Some places enjoy the means of grace in greater plenty, power, and purity, than other places. God is a free agent, and acts so in all his disposals, both as the God of nature and as the God of grace, common and distinguishing grace. By Christ's <hi type="italic">mighty works</hi> they should have been prevailed with, not only to receive his doctrine, but to obey his law; the curing of bodily diseases should have been the healing of their souls, but it had not that effect. Note, The stronger inducements we have to repent, the more heinous is the impenitency and the severer will the reckoning be, for Christ keeps account of the <hi type="italic">mighty works done</hi> among us, and of the gracious works done for us too, by which also we should be <hi type="italic">led to repentance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.4">Rom. ii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen22103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22104" type="x-p"/> (1.) Chorazin and Bethsaida are here instanced (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.21-Matt.11.22">v. 21, 22</reference>), they have each of them their woe: <hi type="italic">Woe unto thee, Chorazin, woe unto thee, Bethsaida.</hi> Christ came <hi type="italic">into the world to bless us;</hi> but if that blessing be slighted, he has woes in reserve, and his woes are of all others the most terrible. These two cities were situate upon <hi type="italic">the sea of Galilee,</hi> the former on the east side, and the latter on the west, rich and populous places; Bethsaida was lately advanced to a city by Philip the tetrarch; out of it Christ took at least three of his apostles: thus highly were these places favoured! Yet because they <hi type="italic">knew not the day of their visitation,</hi> they fell under these woes, which stuck so close to them, that soon after this they decayed, and dwindled into mean, obscure villages. So fatally does sin ruin cities, and so certainly does the word of Christ take place! <div eID="gen22104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22105" type="x-p"/> Now Chorazin and Bethsaida are here compared with Tyre and Sidon, two maritime cities we read much of in the Old Testament, that had been brought to ruin, but began to flourish again; these cities bordered upon Galilee, but were in a very ill name among the Jews for idolatry and other wickedness. Christ sometimes went <hi type="italic">into the coasts of Tyre and Sidon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.21">ch. xv. 21</reference>), but never thither; the Jews would have taken it very heinously if he had; therefore Christ, to convince and humble them, here shows, <div eID="gen22105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22106" type="x-p"/> [1.] That Tyre and Sidon would not have been so bad as Chorazin and Bethsaida. If they had had the same word preached, and the same miracles wrought among them, <hi type="italic">they would have repented,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">long ago,</hi> as Nineveh did, in <hi type="italic">sackcloth and ashes.</hi> Christ, who knows the hearts of all, knew that if he had gone and lived among them, and preached among them, he should have done more good there than where he was; yet he continued where he was for some time, to encourage his ministers to do so, though they see not the success they desire. Note, Among the children of disobedience, some are more easily wrought upon than others; and it is a great aggravation of the impenitency of those who plentifully enjoy the means of grace, not only that there are many who sit under the same means that are wrought upon, but that there are many more that would have been wrought upon, if they had enjoyed the same means. See <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.6-Ezek.3.7">Ezek. iii. 6, 7</reference>. Our repentance is slow and delayed, but theirs would have been speedy; they would have repented long ago. Ours has been slight and superficial; theirs would have been deep and serious, in <hi type="italic">sackcloth and ashes.</hi> Yet we must observe, with an awful adoration of the divine sovereignty, that the Tyrians and Sidonians will justly perish in their sin, though, if they had had the means of grace, they would have repented; for God is a <hi type="italic">debtor to no man.</hi> <div eID="gen22106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22107" type="x-p"/> [2.] That therefore Tyre and Sidon shall not be so miserable as Chorazin and Bethsaida, but it shall be <hi type="italic">more tolerable</hi> for them in the <hi type="italic">day of judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.22">v. 22</reference>. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> At the <hi type="italic">day of judgment</hi> the everlasting state of the children of men will, by an unerring and unalterable doom, be determined; happiness or misery, and the several degrees of each. Therefore it is called the <hi type="italic">eternal judgment</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.6.2">Heb. vi. 2</reference>), because decisive of the eternal state. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> In that judgment, all the means of grace that were enjoyed in the state of probation will certainly come into the account, and it will be enquired, not only how bad we were, but how much better we might have been, had it not been our own fault, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.3-Isa.5.4">Isa. v. 3, 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Though the damnation of all that perish will be intolerable, yet the damnation of those who had the fullest and clearest discoveries made them of the power and grace of Christ, and yet repented not, will be of all others the most intolerable.
