The gospel light and sound open the faculties, and enlarge the capacities of all that see and hear it, either to receive the riches of <hi type="italic">divine grace,</hi> or (if that grace be slighted) to take in the more plentiful effusions of <hi type="italic">divine wrath.</hi> If self-reproach be the torture of hell, it must needs be hell indeed to those who had such a fair opportunity of getting to heaven. <hi type="italic">Son, remember that.</hi> <div eID="gen22107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22108" type="x-p"/> (2.) Capernaum is here condemned with an emphasis (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.23">v. 23</reference>), "<hi type="italic">And thou, Capernaum,</hi> hold up thy hand, and hear they doom," Capernaum, above all the cities of Israel, was dignified with Christ's most usual residence; it was like Shiloh of old, the place which he chose, to put his name there, and it fared with it as with Shiloh, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jer. vii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.14">14</reference>. Christ's miracles here were <hi type="italic">daily bread,</hi> and therefore, as the manna of old, were despised and called light bread. Many a sweet and comfortable lecture of grace Christ had read them to little purpose, and therefore he reads them a dreadful lecture of wrath: those who will not hear the former shall be made to feel the latter. <div eID="gen22108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22109" type="x-p"/> We have here Capernaum's doom, <div eID="gen22109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22110" type="x-p"/> [1.] Put absolutely; Thou <hi type="italic">which art exalted to heaven shalt be brought down to hell</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Those who enjoy the gospel in power and purity, are thereby <hi type="italic">exalted to heaven;</hi> they have therein a great honour for the present, and a great advantage for eternity; they are lifted up toward <hi type="italic">heaven;</hi> but if, notwithstanding, they still <hi type="italic">cleave to the earth,</hi> they may thank themselves that they are not lifted up <hi type="italic">into heaven. Secondly,</hi> Gospel advantages and advancements abused will sink sinners so much lower into hell. Our external privileges will be so far from saving us, that if our hearts and lives be not agreeable to them, they will but inflame the reckoning: the higher the precipice is, the more fatal is the fall from it: Let us <hi type="italic">not therefore be high-minded, but fear;</hi> not slothful, but diligent. See <reference osisRef="Job.20.6-Job.20.7">Job xx. 6, 7</reference>. <div eID="gen22110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22111" type="x-p"/> [2.] We have it here put in comparison with the doom of Sodom—a place more remarkable, both for sin and ruin, than perhaps any other; and yet Christ here tells us, <div eID="gen22111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22112" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> That Capernaum's means would have saved Sodom. If these miracles had been done among the Sodomites, as bad as they were, they would have repented, and <hi type="italic">their city would have remained unto this day</hi> a monument of sparing mercy, as now it is of destroying justice, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.7">Jude 7</reference>. Note, Upon true repentance through Christ, even the greatest sin shall be pardoned and the greatest ruin prevented, that of Sodom not excepted. Angels were sent to Sodom, and yet it remained not; but if Christ had been sent thither, it <hi type="italic">would have remained;</hi> how well is it for us, then, that the world to come is <hi type="italic">put in subjection to Christ,</hi> and <hi type="italic">not to angels!</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.5">Heb. ii. 5</reference>. Lot would not have <hi type="italic">seemed as one that mocked,</hi> if he had wrought miracles. <div eID="gen22112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22113" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That Sodom's ruin will therefore be less at the great day than Capernaum's. Sodom will have many things to answer for, but not the sin of neglecting Christ, as Capernaum will. If the gospel prove <hi type="italic">a savour of death,</hi> a killing savour, it is doubly so; it is <hi type="italic">of death unto death,</hi> so great a death (<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.16">2 Cor. ii. 16</reference>); Christ had said the same of all other places that receive not his ministers nor bid his gospel welcome (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.15">ch. x. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">It shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom than for that city.</hi> We that have now the written word in our hands, the gospel preached, and the gospel ordinances administered to us, and live under the dispensation of the Spirit, have advantages not inferior to those of Chorazin, and Bethsaida, and Capernaum, and the account in the great day will be accordingly. It has therefore been justly said, that the professors of this age, whether they go to heaven or hell, will be the greatest debtors in either of these places; if to heaven, the greatest debtors to divine mercy for those rich means that brought them thither; if to hell, the greatest debtors to divine justice, for those rich means that would have kept them from thence.
entries.50eff2f137c1f1bd75cc101784370ef9f2274c9f: <div eID="gen22113" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Invitation to Burthened Souls.</title> <div sID="gen22114" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> At that time Jesus answered and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them unto babes. <hi type="super">26</hi> Even so, Father: for so it seemed good in thy sight. <hi type="super">27</hi> All things are delivered unto me of my Father: and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and <hi type="italic">he</hi> to whomsoever the Son will reveal <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">28</hi> Come unto me, all <hi type="italic">ye</hi> that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. <hi type="super">29</hi> Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. <hi type="super">30</hi> For my yoke <hi type="italic">is</hi> easy, and my burden is light. <div eID="gen22114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22115" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have Christ looking up to heaven, with thanksgiving to his Father for the sovereignty and security of the covenant of redemption; and looking around him upon this earth, with an offer to all the children of men, to whom these presents shall come, of the privileges and benefits of the covenant of grace. <div eID="gen22115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22116" type="x-p"/> I. Christ here returns thanks to God for his favour to those <hi type="italic">babes</hi> who had the mysteries of the gospel <hi type="italic">revealed to them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.25-Matt.11.26">v. 25, 26</reference>). <hi type="italic">Jesus answered and said.</hi> It is called an answer, though no other words are before recorded but his own, because it is so comfortable a reply to the melancholy considerations preceding, and is aptly set in the balance against them. The sin and ruin of those woeful cities, no doubt, was a grief to the Lord Jesus; he could not but <hi type="italic">weep over</hi> them, as he did <hi type="italic">over Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.41">Luke xix. 41</reference>); with this thought therefore he refreshes himself; and to make it the more refreshing, he puts it into a thanksgiving; that for all this, <hi type="italic">there is a remnant,</hi> though but <hi type="italic">babes,</hi> to whom the things of the gospel are <hi type="italic">revealed. Though Israel be not gathered, yet shall he be glorious.</hi> Note, We may take great encouragement in looking upward to God, when round about us we see nothing but what is discouraging. It is sad to see how regardless most men are of their own happiness, but it is comfortable to think that the wise and faithful God will, however, effectually secure the interests of his own glory. <hi type="italic">Jesus answered and said, I thank thee.</hi> Note, Thanksgiving is a proper answer to dark and disquieting thoughts, and may be an effectual means to silence them. Songs of praise are sovereign cordials to drooping souls, and will help to cure melancholy. When we have no other answer ready to the suggestions of grief and fear, we may have recourse to this, <hi type="italic">I thank thee, O Father;</hi> let us bless God that it is not worse with us than it is. <div eID="gen22116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22117" type="x-p"/> Now in this thanksgiving of Christ, we may observe, <div eID="gen22117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22118" type="x-p"/> 1. The titles he gives to God; <hi type="italic">O Father, Lord of heaven and earth.</hi> Note, (1.) In all our approaches to God, by praise as well as by prayer, it is good for us to eye him as a Father, and to fasten on that relation, not only when we ask for the mercies we want, but when we give thanks for the mercies we have received. Mercies are then doubly sweet, and powerful to enlarge the heart in praise, when they are received as tokens of a Father's love, and gifts of a Father's hand; <hi type="italic">Giving thanks to the Father,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.12">Col. i. 12</reference>. It becomes children to be grateful, and to say, <hi type="italic">Thank you, father,</hi> as readily as, <hi type="italic">Pray, father.</hi> (2.) When we come to God as a Father, we must withal remember, that he is <hi type="italic">Lord of heaven and earth;</hi> which obliges us to come to him with reverence, as to the sovereign Lord of all, and yet with confidence, as one able to do for us whatever we need or can desire; to defend us from all evil and to supply us with all good. Christ, in Melchizedec, had long since <hi type="italic">blessed God</hi> as the Possessor, or <hi type="italic">Lord of heaven and earth;</hi> and in all our thanksgivings for mercies in the stream, we must give him the glory of the all-sufficiency that is in the fountain. <div eID="gen22118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22119" type="x-p"/> 2. The thing he gives thanks for: <hi type="italic">Because thou has hid these things from the wise and prudent, and</hi> yet <hi type="italic">revealed them to babes. These things;</hi> he does not say what things, but means the great things of the gospel, <hi type="italic">the things that belong to our peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.42">Luke xix. 42</reference>. He spoke thus emphatically of them, <hi type="italic">these things,</hi> because they were things that filled him, and should fill us: all other things are as nothing to <hi type="italic">these things.</hi> <div eID="gen22119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22120" type="x-p"/> Note (1.) The great things of the everlasting gospel have been and are hid from many that were <hi type="italic">wise and prudent,</hi> that were eminent for learning and worldly policy; some of the greatest scholars and the greatest statesmen have been the greatest strangers to gospel mysteries. <hi type="italic">The world by wisdom knew not God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.21">1 Cor. i. 21</reference>. Nay, there is an opposition given to the gospel, by a <hi type="italic">science falsely so called,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1 Tim. vi. 20</reference>. Those who are most expert in things sensible and secular, are commonly least experienced in spiritual things. Men may dive deeply into the mysteries of nature and into the mysteries of state, and yet be ignorant of, and mistake about, the mysteries of <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven,</hi> for want of an experience of the power of them. <div eID="gen22120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22121" type="x-p"/> (2.) While <hi type="italic">the wise and prudent men</hi> of the world are in the dark about gospel mysteries, even the <hi type="italic">babes in Christ</hi> have the sanctifying saving knowledge of them: <hi type="italic">Thou hast revealed them unto babes.</hi> Such the disciples of Christ were; men of mean birth and education; no scholars, no artists, no politicians, unlearned and ignorant men, <reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Acts iv. 13</reference>. Thus are the secrets of wisdom, which are double to that which is (<reference osisRef="Job.11.6">Job xi. 6</reference>), made known <hi type="italic">to babes and sucklings,</hi> that <hi type="italic">out of their mouth strength</hi> might be <hi type="italic">ordained</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.2">Ps. viii. 2</reference>), and God's <hi type="italic">praise</hi> thereby <hi type="italic">perfected.</hi> The learned men of the world were not made choice of to be the preachers of the gospel, but <hi type="italic">the foolish things of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.6">1 Cor. ii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.10">10</reference>). <div eID="gen22121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22122" type="x-p"/> (3.) This difference between <hi type="italic">the prudent</hi> and the <hi type="italic">babes</hi> is of God's own making. [1.] It is he that has <hi type="italic">hid these things from the wise and prudent;</hi> he gave them parts, and learning, and much of human understanding above others, and they were proud of that, and rested in it, and looked no further; and therefore God justly denies them the Spirit of wisdom and revelation, and then, though they hear the sound of the gospel tidings, they are to them as a <hi type="italic">strange thing.</hi> God is not the Author of their ignorance and error, but he leaves them to themselves, and their sin becomes their punishment, and the Lord is righteous in it. See <reference osisRef="John.12.39-John.12.40">John xii. 39, 40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.7-Rom.11.8">Rom. xi. 7, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.28.26-Acts.28.27">Acts xxviii. 26, 27</reference>. Had they honoured God with the wisdom and prudence they had, he would have given them the knowledge of these better things; but because they served their lusts with them, he has <hi type="italic">hid their hearts from this understanding.</hi> [2.] It is he that has <hi type="italic">revealed them unto babes.</hi> Things revealed belong to our children (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">Deut. xxix. 29</reference>), and to them he <hi type="italic">gives an understanding</hi> to receive these things, and the impressions of them. Thus <hi type="italic">he resists the proud,</hi> and <hi type="italic">gives grace to the humble,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.4.6">Jam. iv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen22122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22123" type="x-p"/> (4.) This dispensation must be resolved into the divine sovereignty. Christ himself referred it to that; <hi type="italic">Even so, Father, for so it seemed good in thy sight.</hi> Christ here subscribes to the will of his Father in this matter; <hi type="italic">Even so.</hi> Let God take what ways he pleases to glorify himself, and make us of what instruments he pleases for the carrying on of his own work; his grace is his own, and he may give or withhold it as he pleases. We can give no reason why Peter, a fisherman, should be made an apostle, and not Nicodemus, a Pharisee, and a ruler of the Jews, though he also believed in Christ; but <hi type="italic">so it seemed good in God's sight.</hi> Christ said this in the hearing of his disciples, to show them that it was not for any merit of their own that they were thus dignified and distinguished, but purely from God's good pleasure; he made them to differ. <div eID="gen22123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22124" type="x-p"/> (5.) This way of dispensing divine grace is to be acknowledged by us, as it was by our Lord Jesus, with all thankfulness. We must thank God, [1.] That <hi type="italic">these things</hi> are <hi type="italic">revealed;</hi> the mystery hid from ages and generations is manifested; that they are <hi type="italic">revealed,</hi> not to a few, but to be published to all the world. [2.] That they are <hi type="italic">revealed to babes;</hi> that the meek and humble are beautified with this salvation; and this honour put upon those whom the world pours contempt upon. [3.] It magnifies the mercy to them, that <hi type="italic">these things</hi> are <hi type="italic">hid from the wise and prudent:</hi> distinguishing favours are the most obliging. As Job adored <hi type="italic">the name of the Lord</hi> in <hi type="italic">taking away</hi> as well as in <hi type="italic">giving,</hi> so may we in <hi type="italic">hiding these things from the wise and prudent,</hi> as well as in <hi type="italic">revealing them unto babes;</hi> not as it is their misery, but as it is a method by which self is abased, proud thoughts brought down, all flesh silenced, and divine power and wisdom made to shine the more bright. See <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1 Cor. i. 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.31">31</reference>. <div eID="gen22124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22125" type="x-p"/> II. Christ here makes a gracious offer of the benefits of the gospel to all, and these are the things which are <hi type="italic">revealed to babes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.25">v. 25</reference>, &c. Observe here, <div eID="gen22125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22126" type="x-p"/> 1. The solemn preface which ushers in this call or invitation, both to command our attention to it, and to encourage our compliance with it. That we <hi type="italic">might have strong consolation,</hi> in flying for refuge to this <hi type="italic">hope set before us,</hi> Christ prefixes his authority, produces his credentials; we shall see he is empowered to make this offer. <div eID="gen22126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22127" type="x-p"/> Two things he here lays before us, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">v. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen22127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22128" type="x-p"/> (1.) His commission from the Father: <hi type="italic">All things are delivered unto me of my Father.</hi> Christ, as God, is equal in power and glory with the Father; but as Mediator he receives his power and glory from the Father; has <hi type="italic">all judgment committed to him.</hi> He is authorized to settle a new covenant between God and man, and to offer peace and happiness to the apostate world, upon such terms as he should think fit: he was sanctified and sealed to be the sole Plenipotentiary, to concert and establish this great affair. In order to this, he has <hi type="italic">all power</hi> both <hi type="italic">in heaven and in earth,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">ch. xxviii. 18</reference>); power over all flesh (<reference osisRef="John.17.2">John xvii. 2</reference>); authority to execute judgment, <reference osisRef="John.5.22">John v. 22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.27">27</reference>. This encourages us to come to Christ, that he is commissioned to receive us, and to give us what we come for, and has <hi type="italic">all things delivered to him</hi> for that purpose, by him who is <hi type="italic">Lord of all.</hi> All powers, all treasures are in his hand. Observe, The Father has delivered his all into the hands of the Lord Jesus; let us but deliver our all into his hand and the work is done; God has made him the great Referee, the blessed Daysman, to lay his hand upon us both; that which we have to do is to agree to the reference, to submit to the arbitration of the Lord Jesus, for the taking up of this unhappy controversy, and to enter into bonds to stand to his award. <div eID="gen22128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22129" type="x-p"/> (2.) His intimacy with the Father: <hi type="italic">No man knoweth the Son but the Father, Neither knoweth any man the Father save the Son.</hi> This gives us a further satisfaction, and an abundant one. Ambassadors use to have not only their commissions, which they produce, but their instructions, which they reserve to themselves, to be made use of as there is occasion in their negotiations; our Lord Jesus had both, not only authority, but ability, for his undertaking. In transacting the great business of our redemption, the Father and the Son are the parties principally concerned; <hi type="italic">the counsel of peace is between them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 13</reference>. It must therefore be a great encouragement to us to be assured, that they understood one another very well in this affair; that the Father knew the Son, and the Son knew the Father, and both perfectly (a mutual consciousness we may call it, between the Father and the Son), so that there could be no mistake in the settling of this matter; as often there is among men, to the overthrow of contracts, and the breaking of the measures taken, through their misunderstanding one another. The Son had <hi type="italic">lain in the bosom of the Father</hi> from eternity; he was <hi type="italic">&#224; secretioribus—of the cabinet-council,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.18">John i. 18</reference>. He was <hi type="italic">by him, as one brought up with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.8.30">Prov. viii. 30</reference>), so that <hi type="italic">none knows the Father save the Son,</hi> he adds, <hi type="italic">and he to whom the Son will reveal him.</hi> Note, [1.] The happiness of men lies in an acquaintance with God; it <hi type="italic">is life eternal,</hi> it is the perfection of rational beings. [2.] Those who would have an acquaintance with God, must apply themselves to Jesus Christ; for the light of the knowledge of the glory of God shines in the face of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. iv. 6</reference>. We are obliged to Christ for all the revelation we have of God the Father's will and love, ever since Adam sinned; there is no comfortable intercourse between a holy God and sinful man, but in and by a Mediator, <reference osisRef="John.14.6">John xiv. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen22129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22130" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the offer itself that is made to us, and an invitation to accept of it. After so solemn a preface, we may well expect something very great; and it is <hi type="italic">a faithful saying,</hi> and well <hi type="italic">worthy of all acceptation; words whereby we may be saved.</hi> We are here invited to Christ as our Priest, Prince, and Prophet, to be saved, and, in order to that, to be ruled and taught by him. <div eID="gen22130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22131" type="x-p"/> (1.) We must come to Jesus Christ as our Rest, and repose ourselves in him (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">v. 28</reference>), <hi type="italic">Come unto me all ye that labour.</hi> Observe, [1.] The character of the persons invited; <hi type="italic">all that labour, and are heavy laden.</hi> This is a word in season to him that is weary, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Isa. l. 4</reference>. Those who complain of the burthen of the ceremonial law, which was an intolerable yoke, and was made much more so by the tradition of the elders (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.46">Luke xi. 46</reference>), let them come to Christ, and they shall be made easy; he came to free his church from this yoke, to cancel the imposition of those carnal ordinances, and to introduce a purer and more spiritual way of worship; but it is rather to be understood of the burthen of sin, both the guilt and the power of it. Note, All those, and those only, are invited to rest in Christ, that are sensible of sin as a burthen, and groan under it; that are not only convinced of the evil of sin, of their own sin, but are contrite in soul for it; that are really sick of their sins, weary of the service of the world and of the flesh; that see their state sad and dangerous by reason of sin, and are in pain and fear about it, as Ephraim (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.18-Jer.31.20">Jer. xxxi. 18-20</reference>), the prodigal (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.17">Luke xv. 17</reference>), the publican (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.13">Luke xviii. 13</reference>), Peter's hearers (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.37">Acts ii. 37</reference>), Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.9.4">Acts ix. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.9">9</reference>), the jailor (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.29-Acts.16.30">Acts xvi. 29, 30</reference>). This is a necessary preparative for pardon and peace. The Comforter must first convince (<reference osisRef="John.16.8">John xvi. 8</reference>); I have torn and then will heal. [2.] The invitation itself: <hi type="italic">Come unto me.</hi> That glorious display of Christ's greatness which we had (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.27">v. 27</reference>), as Lord of all, might frighten us from him, but see here how he holds out <hi type="italic">the golden sceptre,</hi> that we may touch the top of it and may live. Note, It is the duty and interest of weary <hi type="italic">and heavy laden</hi> sinners to <hi type="italic">come to Jesus Christ.</hi> Renouncing all those things which stand in opposition to him, or in competition with him, we must accept of him, as our Physician and Advocate, and give up ourselves to his conduct and government; freely willing to be saved by him, in his own way, and upon his own terms. <hi type="italic">Come</hi> and <hi type="italic">cast that burden upon</hi> him, under which thou art <hi type="italic">heavy laden.</hi> This is the gospel call, <hi type="italic">The Spirit saith, Come;</hi> and <hi type="italic">the bride saith, Come; let him that is athirst come; Whoever will, let him come.</hi> <div eID="gen22131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22132" type="x-p"/> [3.] The blessing promised to those that do come: <hi type="italic">I will give you rest.</hi> Christ is our Noah, whose name signifies <hi type="italic">rest,</hi> for <hi type="italic">this same shall give us rest.</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.5.29">Gen. v. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.8.9">viii. 9</reference>. Truly <hi type="italic">rest is good</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.15">Gen. xlix. 15</reference>), especially to those <hi type="italic">that labour and are heavy laden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Eccl. v. 12</reference>. Note, Jesus Christ will give assured rest to those weary souls, that by a lively faith come to him for it; <hi type="italic">rest</hi> from the terror of sin, in a well-grounded peace of conscience; <hi type="italic">rest</hi> from the power of sin, in a regular order of the soul, and its due government of itself; a <hi type="italic">rest</hi> in God, and a complacency of soul, in his love. <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6-Ps.11.7">Ps. xi. 6, 7</reference>. This is that <hi type="italic">rest which remains for the people of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.9">Heb. iv. 9</reference>), begun in grace, and perfected in glory. <div eID="gen22132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22133" type="x-p"/> (2.) We must come to Jesus Christ as our Ruler, and submit ourselves to him (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">v. 29</reference>). <hi type="italic">Take my yoke upon you.</hi> This must go along with the former, for Christ is exalted to be both a <hi type="italic">Prince and a Saviour,</hi> a <hi type="italic">Priest upon his throne.</hi> The <hi type="italic">rest</hi> he promises is a release from the drudgery of sin, not from the service of God, but an obligation to the duty we owe to him. Note, Christ has a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> for our necks, as well as a <hi type="italic">crown</hi> for our heads, and this <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> he expects we should <hi type="italic">take upon</hi> us and draw in. To call those who are weary <hi type="italic">and heavy laden,</hi> to <hi type="italic">take a yoke upon</hi> them, looks like adding <hi type="italic">affliction to the afflicted;</hi> but the pertinency of it lies in the word <hi type="italic">my:</hi> "You are under a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> which makes you weary: shake that off and try mine, which will make you easy." Servants are said to be <hi type="italic">under the yoke</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">1 Tim. vi. 1</reference>), and subjects, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.10">1 Kings xii. 10</reference>. To take Christ's <hi type="italic">yoke upon</hi> us, is to put ourselves into the relation to servants and subjects to him, and then of conduct ourselves accordingly, in a conscientious obedience to all his commands, and a cheerful submission to all his disposals: it is to <hi type="italic">obey the gospel of Christ, to yield ourselves to the Lord:</hi> it is Christ's <hi type="italic">yoke;</hi> the <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> he has appointed; a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> he has himself drawn in before us, for <hi type="italic">he learned obedience,</hi> and which he does by his Spirit draw in with us, for <hi type="italic">he helpeth our infirmities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Rom. viii. 26</reference>. A <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> speaks some hardship, but if the beast must draw, the <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> helps him. Christ's commands are all in our favour: we must take this <hi type="italic">yoke upon</hi> us to draw in it. We are yoked to work, and therefore must be diligent; we are yoked to submit, and therefore must be humble and patient: we are yoked together with our fellow-servants, and therefore must keep up the communion of saints: and <hi type="italic">the words of the wise are as goads,</hi> to those who are thus yoked. <div eID="gen22133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22134" type="x-p"/> Now this is the hardest part of our lesson, and therefore it is qualified (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.30">v. 30</reference>). <hi type="italic">My yoke is easy and my burden is light;</hi> you need not be afraid of it. <div eID="gen22134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22135" type="x-p"/> [1.] The <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> of Christ's commands is an <hi type="italic">easy yoke;</hi> it is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">chrestos</hi></hi>, not only <hi type="italic">easy,</hi> but gracious, so the word signifies; it is sweet and pleasant; there is nothing in it to gall the yielding neck, nothing to hurt us, but, on the contrary, must to refresh us. It is a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> that is lined with love. Such is the nature of all Christ's commands, so reasonable in themselves, so profitable to us, and all summed up in one word, and that a sweet word, love. So powerful are the assistances he gives us, so suitable the encouragements, and so strong the consolations, that are to be found in the way of duty, that we may truly say, it is a <hi type="italic">yoke</hi> of pleasantness. It is easy to the new nature, very <hi type="italic">easy to him that understandeth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.14.6">Prov. xiv. 6</reference>. It may be a little hard at first, but it is easy afterwards; the love of God and the hope of heaven will make it <hi type="italic">easy.</hi> <div eID="gen22135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22136" type="x-p"/> [2.] The <hi type="italic">burden</hi> of Christ's cross is a <hi type="italic">light burden,</hi> very <hi type="italic">light:</hi> afflictions from Christ, which befal us as men; afflictions for Christ, which befal us as Christians; the latter are especially meant. This <hi type="italic">burden</hi> in itself is <hi type="italic">not joyous, but grievous;</hi> yet as it is Christ's, it is <hi type="italic">light.</hi> Paul knew as much of it as any man, and he calls it a <hi type="italic">light affliction,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.17">2 Cor. iv. 17</reference>. God's presence (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Isa. xliii. 2</reference>), Christ's sympathy (<reference osisRef="Isa.73.9">Isa. lxxiii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.25">Dan. iii. 25</reference>), and especially the Spirit's aids and comforts (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2 Cor. i. 5</reference>), make suffering for Christ <hi type="italic">light</hi> and <hi type="italic">easy.</hi> As afflictions abound, and are prolonged, consolations abound, and are prolonged too. Let this therefore reconcile us to the difficulties, and help us over the discouragements, we may meet with, both in doing work and suffering work; though we may lose <hi type="italic">for</hi> Christ, we shall not lose <hi type="italic">by him.</hi> <div eID="gen22136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22137" type="x-p"/> (3.) We must come to Jesus Christ as our Teacher, and set ourselves to learn of him, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">v. 29</reference>. Christ has erected a great school, and has invited us to be his scholars. We must enter ourselves, associate with his scholars, and daily attend the instructions he gives by his word and Spirit. We must converse much with what he said, and have it ready to use upon all occasions; we must conform to what he did, and follow his steps, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.21">1 Pet. ii. 21</reference>. Some make the following words, <hi type="italic">for I am meek and lowly in heart,</hi> to be the particular lesson we are required to learn from the example of Christ. We must learn of him to be <hi type="italic">meek</hi> and <hi type="italic">lowly,</hi> and must mortify our pride and passion, which render us so unlike to him. We must so <hi type="italic">learn of Christ</hi> as to <hi type="italic">learn Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.20">Eph. iv. 20</reference>), for he is both Teacher and Lesson, Guide and Way, and All in All. <div eID="gen22137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22138" type="x-p"/> Two reasons are given why we must <hi type="italic">learn of Christ.</hi> <div eID="gen22138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22139" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">I am meek and lowly in heart,</hi> and therefore fit to teach you. <div eID="gen22139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22140" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">meek,</hi> and can have <hi type="italic">compassion on the ignorant,</hi> whom others would be in a passion with. Many able teachers are hot and hasty, which is a great discouragement to those who are dull and slow; but Christ knows how to bear with such, and to open their understandings. His carriage towards his twelve disciples was a specimen of this; he was mild and gentle with them, and made the best of them; though they were heedless and forgetful, he was not extreme to mark their follies. <hi type="italic">Secondly, He is lowly in heart.</hi> He condescends to teach poor scholars, to teach novices; he chose disciples, not from the court, nor the schools, but from the seaside. He teaches the first principles, such things as are milk for babes; he stoops to the meanest capacities; he taught Ephraim to go, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.3">Hos. xi. 3</reference>. Who teaches like him? It is an encouragement to us to put ourselves to school to such a Teacher. This humility and meekness, as it qualifies him to be a Teacher, so it will be the best qualification of those who are to be taught by him; <hi type="italic">for the meek will he guide in judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Ps. xxv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen22140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22141" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">You shall find rest to your souls.</hi> This promise is borrowed from <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer. vi. 16</reference>, for Christ delighted to express himself in the language of the prophets, to show the harmony between the two Testaments. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Rest for the soul is the most desirable rest; to have the soul to <hi type="italic">dwell at ease. Secondly,</hi> The only way, and a sure way to find <hi type="italic">rest for our souls</hi> is, to sit at Christ's feet and hear his word. The way of duty is the way of rest. The <hi type="italic">understanding</hi> finds <hi type="italic">rest</hi> in the <hi type="italic">knowledge of</hi> God and Jesus Christ, and is there abundantly satisfied, finding <hi type="italic">that</hi> wisdom in the gospel which has been sought for in vain throughout the whole creation, <reference osisRef="Job.28.12">Job xxviii. 12</reference>. The truths Christ teaches are such as we may venture our souls upon. The affections find rest in the love of God and Jesus Christ, and meet with that in them which gives them an abundant satisfaction; quietness and assurance for ever. And those satisfactions will be perfected and perpetuated in heaven, where we shall see and enjoy God immediately, shall see him as he is, and enjoy him as he is ours. This rest is to be had with Christ for all those who learn of him. <div eID="gen22141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22142" type="x-p"/> Well, this is the sum and substance of the gospel call and offer: we are here told, in a few words, what the Lord Jesus requires of us, and it agrees with what God said of him once and again. <hi type="italic">This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, hear ye him.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.11"/> <div eID="gen22142" type="x-p"/>

entries.7f24669b8664ad1e61f52c532bfd1e07f77a25e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13527"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.11.1-Matt.11.19">Mt 11:1-19</reference>. The Imprisoned Baptist's Message to His Master--The Reply, and Discourse, on the Departure of the Messengers, Regarding John and His Mission. ( = <reference osisRef="Luke.7.18-Luke.7.35">Lu 7:18-35</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25877" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13527"/><hi type="bold">1. And it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end of commanding his twelve disciple--</hi>rather, "the twelve disciples,"<div eID="gen25877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he departed thence to teach and to preach in their cities--</hi>This was scarcely a fourth circuit--if we may judge from the less formal way in which it was expressed--but, perhaps, a set of visits paid to certain places, either not reached at all before, or too rapidly passed through, in order to fill up the time till the return of the Twelve. As to their labors, nothing is said of them by our Evangelist. But Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.6">Lu 9:6</reference>) says, "They departed, and went through, the towns," or "villages," "preaching the Gospel, and healing everywhere." Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.12">Mr 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.13">13</reference>), as usual, is more explicit: "And they went out, and preached that men should repent. And they cast out many devils (demons) and anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them." Though this "anointing with oil" was not mentioned in our Lord's instructions--at least in any of the records of them--we know it to have been practiced long after this in the apostolic Church (see <reference osisRef="Jas.5.14">Jas 5:14</reference>, and compare <reference osisRef="Mark.6.12">Mr 6:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.6.13">13</reference>)--not medicinally, but as a sign of the healing virtue which was communicated by their hands, and a symbol of something still more precious. It was unction, indeed, but, as Bengel remarks, it was something very different from what Romanists call extreme unction. He adds, what is very probable, that they do not appear to have carried the oil about with them, but, as the Jews used oil as a medicine, to have employed it just as they found it with the sick, in their own higher way. <div eID="gen25878" type="x-p"/>
entries.696cbc613c5bd6a743565491a024c0766f59d94e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13528"/><div sID="gen25879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13528"/><hi type="bold">2. Now when John had heard in the prison--</hi>For the account of this imprisonment, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.6.17-Mark.6.20">Mr 6:17-20</reference>.<div eID="gen25879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the works of Christ, he sent, &c.--</hi>On the whole passage, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.7.18-Luke.7.35">Lu 7:18-35</reference>.<div eID="gen25880" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.11.20-Matt.11.30">Mt 11:20-30</reference>. Outburst of Feeling Suggested to the Mind of Jesus by the Result of His Labors in Galilee.</title> <div sID="gen25881" type="x-p"/> The connection of this with what goes before it and the similarity of its tone make it evident, we think, that it was delivered on the same occasion, and that it is but a new and more comprehensive series of reflections in the same strain. <div eID="gen25881" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ff5ae8bff64f97232d8687228e371b0df66e49a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13529"/><div sID="gen25882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13529"/>20. Then began he to upbraid the cities wherein most of his mighty works were done, because they repented not. <div eID="gen25882" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a8cd4bf90b35fad1b76f28a509a0f83e58f2010: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13530"/><div sID="gen25883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13530"/><hi type="bold">21. Woe unto thee, Chorazin!--</hi>not elsewhere mentioned, but it must have lain near Capernaum.<div eID="gen25883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25884" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">woe unto thee, Bethsaida--</hi>"fishing-house," a fishing station--on the western side of the Sea of Galilee, and to the north of Capernaum; the birthplace of three of the apostles--the brothers Andrew and Peter, and Philip. These two cities appear to be singled out to denote the whole region in which they lay--a region favored with the Redeemer's presence, teaching, and works above every other.<div eID="gen25884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for if the mighty works--</hi>the miracles<div eID="gen25885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which were done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon--</hi>ancient and celebrated commercial cities, on the northeastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea, lying north of Palestine, and the latter the northernmost. As their wealth and prosperity engendered luxury and its concomitant evils--irreligion and moral degeneracy--their overthrow was repeatedly foretold in ancient prophecy, and once and again fulfilled by victorious enemies. Yet they were rebuilt, and at this time were in a flourishing condition.<div eID="gen25886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25887" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes--</hi>remarkable language, showing that they had done less violence to conscience, and so, in God's sight, were less criminal than the region here spoken of. <div eID="gen25887" type="x-p"/>
entries.74b8a21465cba75558ba20b90354ed03eba0bc73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13531"/><div sID="gen25888" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13531"/><hi type="bold">22. But I say unto you, It shall be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment, than for you--</hi>more endurable. <div eID="gen25888" type="x-p"/>
entries.c0cd7da00177a19a2bd512fb3477d5332e6bfd73: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13532"/><div sID="gen25889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13532"/><hi type="bold">23. And thou, Capernaum--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">Mt 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen25889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which art exalted unto heaven--</hi>Not even of Chorazin and Bethsaida is this said. For since at Capernaum Jesus had His stated abode during the whole period of His public life which He spent in Galilee, it was the most favored spot upon earth, the most exalted in privilege.<div eID="gen25890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be brought down to hell: for if the mighty works, which have been done in thee, had been done in Sodom--</hi>destroyed for its pollutions.<div eID="gen25891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it would have remained until this day--</hi>having done no such violence to conscience, and so incurred unspeakably less guilt. <div eID="gen25892" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a5474f123f6eeb9958e9011bcf5b3270bdaa05e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13533"/><div sID="gen25893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13533"/><hi type="bold">24. But I say unto you, That it shall be more tolerable for the land of Sodom in the day of judgment, than for thee--</hi>"It has been indeed," says Dr. Stanley, "more tolerable, in one sense, in the day of its earthly judgment, for the land of Sodom than for Capernaum; for the name, and perhaps even the remains of Sodom are still to be found on the shores of the Dead Sea; while that of Capernaum has, on the Lake of Gennesareth, been utterly lost." But the judgment of which our Lord here speaks is still future; a judgment not on material cities, but their responsible inhabitants--a judgment final and irretrievable. <div eID="gen25893" type="x-p"/>
entries.800cc649d905d709ac4b0e6c4f9dcfde45036707: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13534"/><div sID="gen25894" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13534"/><hi type="bold">25. At that time Jesus answered and said--</hi>We are not to understand by this, that the previous discourse had been concluded, and that this is a record only of something said about the same period. For the connection is most close, and the word "answered"--which, when there is no one to answer, refers to something just before said, or rising in the mind of the speaker in consequence of something said--confirms this. What Jesus here "answered" evidently was the melancholy results of His ministry, lamented over in the foregoing verses. It is as if He had said, "Yes; but there is a brighter side to the picture; even in those who have rejected the message of eternal life, it is the pride of their own hearts only which has blinded them, and the glory of the truth does but the more appear in their inability to receive it. Nor have all rejected it even here; souls thirsting for salvation have drawn water with joy from the wells of salvation; the weary have found rest; the hungry have been filled with good things, while the rich have been sent empty away."<div eID="gen25894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I thank thee--</hi>rather, "I assent to thee." But this is not strong enough. The idea of "full" or "cordial" concurrence is conveyed by the preposition. The thing expressed is adoring acquiescence, holy satisfaction with that law of the divine procedure about to be mentioned. And as, when He afterwards uttered the same words, He "exulted in spirit" (see on <reference osisRef="Luke.10.21">Lu 10:21</reference>), probably He did the same now, though not recorded.<div eID="gen25895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">O Father, Lord of heaven and earth--</hi>He so styles His Father here, to signify that from Him of right emanates all such high arrangements.<div eID="gen25896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because thou hast hid these things--</hi>the knowledge of these saving truths.<div eID="gen25897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25898" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the wise and prudent--</hi>The former of these terms points to the men who pride themselves upon their speculative or philosophical attainments; the latter to the men of worldly shrewdness--the clever, the sharp-witted, the men of affairs. The distinction is a natural one, and was well understood. (See <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">1Co 1:19</reference>, &c.). But why had the Father hid from such the things that belonged to their peace, and why did Jesus so emphatically set His seal to this arrangement? Because it is not for the offending and revolted to speak or to speculate, but to listen to Him from whom we have broken loose, that we may learn whether there be any recovery for us at all; and if there be, on what principles--of what nature--to what ends. To bring our own "wisdom and prudence" to such questions is impertinent and presumptuous; and if the truth regarding them, or the glory of it, be "hid" from us, it is but a fitting retribution, to which all the right-minded will set their seal along with Jesus.<div eID="gen25898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hast revealed them unto babes--</hi>to babe-like men; men of unassuming docility, men who, conscious that they know nothing, and have no right to sit in judgment on the things that belong to their peace, determine simply to "hear what God the Lord will speak." Such are well called "babes." (See <reference osisRef="Heb.5.13">He 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.11">1Co 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.20">14:20</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen25899" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd4516297326e554da3a309748042a8234270929: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13535"/><div sID="gen25900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13535"/><hi type="bold">26. Even so, Father; for so it seemed good--</hi>the emphatic and chosen term for expressing any object of divine complacency; whether Christ Himself (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.17">Mt 3:17</reference>), or God's gracious eternal arrangements (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.2.13">Php 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen25900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thy sight--</hi>This is just a sublime echo of the foregoing words; as if Jesus, when He uttered them, had paused to reflect on it, and as if the glory of it--not so much in the light of its own reasonableness as of God's absolute will that so it should be--had filled His soul. <div eID="gen25901" type="x-p"/>
entries.afffb63342f23ce5b545c9dc59c7f247fc184c22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13536"/><div sID="gen25902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13536"/><hi type="bold">27. All things are delivered unto me of my Father--</hi>He does not say, They are revealed--as to one who knew them not, and was an entire stranger to them save as they were discovered to Him--but, They are "delivered over," or "committed," to Me of My Father; meaning the whole administration of the kingdom of grace. So in <reference osisRef="John.3.35">Joh 3:35</reference>, "The Father loveth the Son, and hath given all things into His hand" (see on <reference osisRef="John.3.35">Joh 3:35</reference>). But though the "all things" in both these passages refer properly to the kingdom of grace, they of course include all things necessary to the full execution of that trust--that is, unlimited power. (So <reference osisRef="Matt.28.18">Mt 28:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.2">Joh 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.22">Ep 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen25902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and no man knoweth the Son, but the Father; neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whomsoever the Son will--</hi>willeth<div eID="gen25903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to reveal him--</hi>What a saying is this, that "the Father and the Son are mutually and exclusively known to each other!" A higher claim to equality with the Father cannot be conceived. Either, then, we have here one of the revolting assumptions ever uttered, or the proper divinity of Christ should to Christians be beyond dispute. "But, alas for me!" may some burdened soul, sighing for relief, here exclaim. If it be thus with us, what can any poor creature do but lie down in passive despair, unless he could dare to hope that he may be one of the favored class "to whom the Son is willing to reveal the Father." But nay. This testimony to the sovereignty of that gracious "will," on which alone men's salvation depends, is designed but to reveal the source and enhance the glory of it when once imparted--not to paralyze or shut the soul up in despair. Hear, accordingly, what follows: <div eID="gen25904" type="x-p"/>
entries.b75e17ebd0e11b4c3158da290a6f7a0aef995fbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13537"/><div sID="gen25905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13537"/><hi type="bold">28. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest--</hi>Incomparable, ravishing sounds these--if ever such were heard in this weary, groaning world! What gentleness, what sweetness is there in the very style of the invitation--"Hither to Me"; and in the words, "All ye that toil and are burdened," the universal wretchedness of man is depicted, on both its sides--the active and the passive forms of it. <div eID="gen25905" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c99cb4022c4fc685d367cbfe3d0ccd35036c054: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13538"/><div sID="gen25906" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13538"/><hi type="bold">29. Take my yoke upon you--</hi>the yoke of subjection to Jesus.<div eID="gen25906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls--</hi>As Christ's willingness to empty Himself to the uttermost of His Father's requirements was the spring of ineffable repose to His own Spirit, so in the same track does He invite all to follow Him, with the assurance of the same experience. <div eID="gen25907" type="x-p"/>
entries.bfbc166692743cb5fbbcb6259efe227a5420157a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13539"/><div sID="gen25908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13539"/><hi type="bold">30. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light--</hi>Matchless paradox, even among the paradoxically couched maxims in which our Lord delights! That rest which the soul experiences when once safe under Christ's wing makes all yokes easy, all burdens light. <chapter eID="Matt.11"/>

entries.c1158e05f87280f140c81f0fcbe8cb9d2ce03d19: <div eID="gen37125" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen37126" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37127" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37127" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37126" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37128" type="x-p"/> Christ, having finished his instructions to his disciples, departs to preach in different cities, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.1">Mat 11:1</reference>. John sends two of his disciples to him to inquire whether he were the Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.2-Mat.11.6">Mat 11:2-6</reference>. Christ's testimony concerning John, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.7-Mat.11.15">Mat 11:7-15</reference>. He upbraids the Jews with their capriciousness, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.16-Mat.11.19">Mat 11:16-19</reference>. The condemnation of Chorazin, and Bethsaida, and Capernaum, for their unbelief and impenitence, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.20-Mat.11.24">Mat 11:20-24</reference>. Praises the Divine wisdom for revealing the Gospel to the simple-hearted, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.25">Mat 11:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.26">Mat 11:26</reference>. Shows that none can know God but by the revelation of his Son, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.27">Mat 11:27</reference>. Invites the distressed to come unto him, and gives them the promise of rest for their souls, <reference osisRef="Mat.11.29-Mat.11.30">Mat 11:29-30</reference>. <div eID="gen37128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37129" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen37129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37130" type="x-p"/> This verse properly belongs to the preceding chapter, from which it should on no account be separated; as with that it has the strictest connection, but with this it has none. <div eID="gen37130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37131" type="x-p"/> To teach and to preach - To teach, to give private instructions to as many as came unto him; and to preach, to proclaim publicly, that the kingdom of God is at hand; two grand parts of the duty of a Gospel minister. <div eID="gen37131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37132" type="x-p"/> Their cities - The cities of the Jews.
entries.844facbd40a9cb5d4d9606f6e31b7d4685d8ce78: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen37132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37133" type="x-p"/> John had heard in the prison - John was cast into prison by order of Herod Antipas, <reference osisRef="Mat.14.3">Mat 14:3</reference>, etc., (where see the notes), a little after our Lord began his public ministry, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.12">Mat 4:12</reference>; and after the first passover, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.24">Joh 3:24</reference>.
entries.c02d0e522cfbd04878d2f2d8a76954ef613dc4d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen37133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37134" type="x-p"/> Art thou he that should come - Ο ερχομενος, he that cometh, seems to have been a proper name of the Messiah; to save or deliver is necessarily implied. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.7.19">Luk 7:19</reference> (note). <div eID="gen37134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37135" type="x-p"/> There is some difficulty in what is here spoken of John. Some have thought he was utterly ignorant of our Lord's Divine mission, and that he sent merely for his own information; but this is certainly inconsistent with his own declaration, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.15">Luk 3:15</reference>, etc.; <reference osisRef="Joh.1.15">Joh 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.26">Joh 1:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.33">Joh 1:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joh.3.28">Joh 3:28</reference>, etc. Others suppose he sent the message merely for the instruction of his disciples; that, as he saw his end approaching, he wished them to have the fullest conviction that Jesus was the Messiah, that they might attach themselves to him. <div eID="gen37135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37136" type="x-p"/> A third opinion takes a middle course between the two former, and states that, though John was at first perfectly convinced that Jesus was the Christ, yet, entertaining some hopes that he would erect a secular kingdom in Judea, wished to know whether this was likely to take place speedily. It is very probable that John now began, through the length of his confinement, to entertain doubts, relative to his kingdom, which perplexed and harassed his mind; and he took the most reasonable way to get rid of them at once, viz. by applying to Christ himself. <div eID="gen37136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37137" type="x-p"/> Two of his disciples - Instead of δυο, two, several excellent MSS., with both the Syriac, Armenian, Gothic, and one copy of the Itala, have δια, by; he sent by his disciples.
entries.80aaf13de128a24c0959d2af83ced75694f10422: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen37137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37138" type="x-p"/> Go and show John the things - ye do hear and see - Christ would have men to judge only of him and of others by their works. This is the only safe way of judging. A man is not to be credited because he professes to know such and such things; but because he demonstrates by his conduct that his pretensions are not vain.
entries.6bf81bf36b5d80407466535a24736535b23f1bba: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen37138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37139" type="x-p"/> The blind receive their sight, etc. - Αναβλεπωσι, look upwards, contemplating the heavens which their Lord hath made. <div eID="gen37139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37140" type="x-p"/> The lame walk - Περιπατωσι, they walk about; to give the fullest proof to the multitude that their cure was real. These miracles were not only the most convincing proofs of the supreme power of Christ, but were also emblematic of that work of salvation which he effects in the souls of men. <div eID="gen37140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37141" type="x-p"/> 1. Sinners are blind; their understanding is so darkened by sin that they see not the way of truth and salvation. <div eID="gen37141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37142" type="x-p"/> 2. They are lame - not able to walk in the path of righteousness. <div eID="gen37142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37143" type="x-p"/> 3. They are leprous, their souls are defiled with sin, the most loathsome and inveterate disease; deepening in themselves, and infecting others. <div eID="gen37143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37144" type="x-p"/> 4. They are deaf to the voice of God, his word, and their own conscience. <div eID="gen37144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37145" type="x-p"/> 5. They are dead in trespasses and sins; God, who is the life of the soul, being separated from it by iniquity. <div eID="gen37145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37146" type="x-p"/> Nothing less than the power of Christ can redeem from all this; and, from all this, that power of Christ actually does redeem every penitent believing soul. Giving sight to the blind, and raising the dead, are allowed by the ancient rabbins to be works which the Messiah should perform, when he should manifest himself in Israel. <div eID="gen37146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37147" type="x-p"/> The poor have the Gospel preached to them - And what was this Gospel? Why, the glad tidings that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners: that he opens the eyes of the blind; enables the lame to walk with an even, steady, and constant pace in the way of holiness; cleanses the lepers from all the defilement of their sins; opens the ears of the deaf to hear his pardoning words; and raises those who were dead in trespasses and sins to live in union with himself to all eternity.
entries.14d622f280838a21f4d01c3fd1960277b649e9ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen37147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37148" type="x-p"/> Blessed is he whosoever shall not be offended in me - Or, Happy is he who will not be stumbled at me; for the word σκανδαλιζεσθαι, in its root, signifies to hit against or stumble over a thing, which one may meet with in the way. The Jews, as was before remarked, expected a temporal deliverer. Many might he tempted to reject Christ, because of his mean appearance, etc., and so lose the benefit of salvation through him. To instruct and caution such, our blessed Lord spoke these words. By his poverty and meanness he condemns the pride and pomp of this world. He who will not humble himself, and become base, and poor, and vile in his own eyes, cannot enter into the kingdom of God. It is the poor, in general, who hear the Gospel; the rich and the great are either too busy, or too much gratified with temporal things, to pay any attention to the voice of God.
entries.7a9d2ad4d87e32c489fe65662d811eb7c0fdf47d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen37148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37149" type="x-p"/> What went ye out into the wilderness to see? - The purport of our Lord's design, in this and the following verses, is to convince the scribes and Pharisees of the inconsistency of their conduct in acknowledging John Baptist for a divinely authorized teacher, and not believing in the very Christ which he pointed out to them. He also shows, from the excellencies of John's character, that their confidence in him was not misplaced, and that this was a farther argument why they should have believed in him, whom the Baptist proclaimed as being far superior to himself. <div eID="gen37149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37150" type="x-p"/> A reed shaken with the wind? - An emblem of an irresolute, unsteady mind, which believes and speaks one thing to-day, and another to-morrow. Christ asks these Jews if they had ever found any thing in John like this: Was he not ever steady and uniform in the testimony he bore to me? The first excellency which Christ notices in John was his steadiness; convinced once of the truth, he continued to believe and assert it. This is essentially necessary to every preacher, and to every private Christian. He who changes about from opinion to opinion, and from one sect or party to another, is never to be depended on; there is much reason to believe that such a person is either mentally weak, or has never been rationally and divinely convinced of the truth.
entries.a6a051825e45ac66b7c86b7d0a00a2774a025dd1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen37150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37151" type="x-p"/> A man clothed in soft raiment? - A second excellency in John was, his sober and mortified life. A preacher of the Gospel should have nothing about him which savours of effeminacy and worldly pomp: he is awfully mistaken who thinks to prevail on the world to hear him and receive the truth, by conforming himself to its fashions and manners. Excepting the mere color of his clothes, we can scarcely now distinguish a preacher of the Gospel, whether in the establishment of the country, or out of it, from the merest worldly man. Ruffles, powder, and fribble seem universally to prevail. Thus the Church and the world begin to shake hands, the latter still retaining its enmity to God. How can those who profess to preach the doctrine of the cross act in this way? Is not a worldly-minded preacher, in the most peculiar sense, an abomination in the eyes of the Lord? <div eID="gen37151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37152" type="x-p"/> Are in kings' houses - A third excellency in John was, he did not affect high things. He was contented to live in the desert, and to announce the solemn and severe truths of his doctrine to the simple inhabitants of the country. Let it be well observed, that the preacher who conforms to the world in his clothing, is never in his element but when he is frequenting the houses and tables of the rich and great.
entries.291c34235a0e971151619e3a8a9cdd51f9f56d33: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen37152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37153" type="x-p"/> A prophet? yea - and more than a prophet - That is, one more excellent (περισσοτερον) than a prophet; one greatly beyond all who had come before him, being the immediate forerunner of Christ, (see below), and who was especially commissioned to prepare the way of the Lord. <div eID="gen37153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37154" type="x-p"/> This was a fourth excellency: he was a prophet, a teacher, a man divinely commissioned to point out Jesus and his salvation; and more excellent than any of the old prophets, because he not only pointed out this Christ, but saw him, and had the honor of dying for that sacred truth which he steadily believed and boldly proclaimed.
entries.fa3623cd31ed68f08177b2467e9b3cc76250fa04: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen37154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37155" type="x-p"/> Behold, I send my messenger - A fifth excellency of the Baptist was, his preparing the way of the Lord; being the instrument, in God's hand, of preparing the people's hearts to receive the Lord Jesus; and it was probably through his preaching that so many thousands attached themselves to Christ, immediately on his appearing as a public teacher.
entries.422bb9fc0d7464d24f598c9ebb688bfb575652ae: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen37155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37156" type="x-p"/> A greater than John the Baptist - A sixth excellency of the Baptist - he was greater than any prophet from the beginning of the world till that time: - 1st. Because he was prophesied of by them, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal 3:1</reference>, where Jesus Christ himself seems to be the speaker. 2ndly. Because he had the privilege of showing the fulfillment of their predictions, by pointing out that Christ has now come, which they foretold should come. And 3dly. Because he saw and enjoyed that salvation which they could only foretell. See Quesnel. <div eID="gen37156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37157" type="x-p"/> Notwithstanding, he that is least in the kingdom of heaven - By the kingdom of heaven in this verse is meant, the fullness of the blessings of the Gospel of peace; which fullness was not known till after Christ had been crucified, and had risen from the dead. Now the least in this kingdom, the meanest preacher of a crucified, risen, and glorified Savior, was greater than John, who was not permitted to live to see the plenitude of Gospel grace, in the pouring out of the Holy Spirit. Let the reader observe, 1st. That the kingdom of heaven here does not mean the state of future glory. See <reference osisRef="Mat.3.2">Mat 3:2</reference>. 2dly. That it is not in holiness or devotedness to God that the least in this kingdom is greater than John; but 3dly. That it is merely in the difference of the ministry. <div eID="gen37157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37158" type="x-p"/> The prophets pointed out a Christ that was coming; John showed that that Christ was then among them; and the preachers of the Gospel prove that this Christ has suffered, and entered into his glory, and that repentance and remission of sins are proclaimed through his blood. There is a saying similar to this among the Jews: "Even the servant maid that passed through the Red Sea, saw what neither Ezekiel, nor any other of the prophets had seen."
entries.5875405b67574eae8c09a74222d1f423b45270e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen37158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37159" type="x-p"/> The kingdom of heaven suffereth violence - The tax-gatherers and heathens, whom the scribes and Pharisees think have no right to the kingdom of the Messiah, filled with holy zeal and earnestness, seize at once on the proffered mercy of the Gospel, and so take the kingdom as by force from those learned doctors who claimed for themselves the chiefest places in that kingdom. Christ himself said, The tax-gatherers and harlots go before you into the kingdom of God. See the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Luk.7.28-Luk.7.30">Luk 7:28-30</reference>. He that will take, get possession of the kingdom of righteousness, peace, and spiritual joy, must be in earnest: all hell will oppose him in every step he takes; and if a man be not absolutely determined to give up his sins and evil companions, and have his soul saved at all hazards, and at every expense, he will surely perish everlastingly. This requires a violent earnestness.
entries.959d41e21cc04dc33c7d6dd73eb70eebaee94d35: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen37159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37160" type="x-p"/> All the prophets and the law prophesied until John - I believe προεφητευσαν means here, they taught, or continued to instruct. They were the instructers concerning the Christ who was to come, till John came and showed that all the predictions of the one, and the types and ceremonies of the other were now about to be fully and finally accomplished; for Christ was now revealed. The word is taken in this sense, <reference osisRef="Mat.7.22">Mat 7:22</reference>.
entries.cf6b0575ec7ba556bb105d1833651de391b9d6ab: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen37160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37161" type="x-p"/> This is Elias, which was for to come - This should always be written Elijah, that as strict a conformity as possible might be kept up between the names in the Old Testament and the New. The Prophet Malachi, who predicted the coming of the Baptist in the spirit and power of Elijah, gave the three following distinct characteristics of him. First, That he should be the forerunner and messenger of the Messiah: Behold I send my messenger before me, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal 3:1</reference>. Secondly, That he should appear before the destruction of the second temple: Even the Lord whom ye seek shall suddenly come to his temple, ibid. Thirdly, That he should preach repentance to the Jews; and that, some time after, the great and terrible day of the Lord should come, and the Jewish land be smitten with a curse, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.5">Mal 4:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.6">Mal 4:6</reference>. Now these three characters agree perfectly with the conduct of the Baptist, and what shortly followed his preaching, and have not been found in any one else; which is a convincing proof that Jesus was the promised Messiah.
entries.cb8aa61f3f94b6b617bc5a6346b99c2e734e4d61: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen37161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37162" type="x-p"/> He that hath ears to hear, let him hear - As if our Lord had said, These things are so clear and manifest that a man has only to hear them to be convinced and fully satisfied of their truth. But neither the Jews of that time nor of the succeeding times to the present day, have heard or considered, these things. When spoken to on these subjects, their common custom is to stop their ears, spit out, and blaspheme; this shows not only a bad, but a ruined cause. They are deeply and willfully blind. They will not come unto the light, lest their deeds should become manifest, that they are not wrought in God. They have ears but they will not hear.
entries.fae8e4532aaba62f0c416442ddddf3ced88cfac5: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen37162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37163" type="x-p"/> But whereunto shall I liken this generation? - That is, the Jewish people - την γενεαν ταυτην, this race: and so the word γενεα is often to be understood in the evangelists. <div eID="gen37163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37164" type="x-p"/> In the markets - Or, places of concourse, αγοραις, from αγειρω, I gather together; not a market-place only, but any place of public resort: probably meaning here, places of public amusement. <div eID="gen37164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37165" type="x-p"/> Calling unto their fellows - Or, companions. Instead of εταιροις, companions, many of the best MSS. have ετεροις, others. The great similarity of the words might have easily produced this difference. <div eID="gen37165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37166" type="x-p"/> There are some to whom every thing is useful in leading them to God; others, to whom nothing is sufficient. Every thing is good to an upright mind, every thing bad to a vicious heart.
entries.aab39d99a53bd23d167b998abcabcd54aaa23f0a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen37166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37167" type="x-p"/> We have piped unto you, and ye have not danced - We have begun the music, which should have been followed by the dance, but ye have not attended to it. <div eID="gen37167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37168" type="x-p"/> We have mourned - and ye have not lamented - Ye have not smote the breast: ουκ εκοψασθε, from κοπτομαι, to strike, or beat the breasts with the hands, particularly in lamentation. So used, <reference osisRef="Nah.2.7">Nah 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.18.13">Luk 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.23.48">Luk 23:48</reference>, and by the best Greek and Roman writers. There is an allusion here to those funeral lamentations explained <reference osisRef="Mat.9.23">Mat 9:23</reference>.
entries.f1206be9506144bd6a32e5daa2377662af7a4f51: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen37168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37169" type="x-p"/> For John came neither eating nor drinking - Leading a very austere and mortified life: and yet, he did not receive him. A sinner will not be persuaded that what he has no mind to imitate can come from God. There are some who will rather blame holiness itself, than esteem it in those whom they do not like. <div eID="gen37169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37170" type="x-p"/> He hath a devil - He is a vile hypocrite, influenced by a demon to deceive and destroy the simple.
entries.b8c11294f29c03fdae13bbd5ec08723064d53d8f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen37170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37171" type="x-p"/> The Son of man came eating and drinking - That is, went wheresoever he was invited to eat a morsel of bread, and observed no rigid fasts: how could he, who had no corrupt appetites to mortify or subdue? <div eID="gen37171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37172" type="x-p"/> They say, Behold a man gluttonous, etc. - Whatever measures the followers of God may take, they will not escape the censure of the world: the best way is not to be concerned at them. Iniquity, being always ready to oppose and contradict the Divine conduct, often contradicts and exposes itself. <div eID="gen37172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37173" type="x-p"/> But wisdom is justified of her children - Those who follow the dictates of true wisdom ever justify, point out as excellent, the holy maxims by which they are guided, for they find the way pleasantness, and the path, peace. Of, here, and in many places of our translation, ought to be written by in modern English. Some suppose that our blessed Lord applies the epithet of η σοφια, that Wisdom to himself; as he does that of Son of man, in the first clause of the verse: and that this refers to the sublime description given of wisdom in Proverbs 8. Others have supposed that by the children or sons (τεκνων) of wisdom our Lord means John Baptist and himself, who came to preach the doctrines of true wisdom to the people, and who were known to be teachers come from God by all those who seriously attended to their ministry: they recommending themselves, by the purity of their doctrines, and the holiness of their lives, to every man's conscience in the sight of God. It is likely, however, that by children our Lord simply means the fruits or effects of wisdom, according to the Hebrew idiom, which denominates the fruits or effects of a thing, its children. So in <reference osisRef="Job.5.7">Job 5:7</reference>, sparks emitted by coals are termed בני רשף beney resheph, the children of the coal. It was probably this well known meaning of the word, which led the Codex Vaticanus, one of the most ancient MSS. in the world, together with the Syriac, Persic, Coptic, and Ethiopic, to read εργων, works, instead of τεκνων, sons or children. Wisdom is vindicated by her works, i.e. the good effects prove that the cause is excellent. <div eID="gen37173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37174" type="x-p"/> The children of true wisdom can justify all God's ways in their salvation; as they know that all the dispensations of Providence work together for the good of those who love and fear God. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.7.35">Luk 7:35</reference> (note).
entries.36639d5ebf7056359f5f1572551904b5bf3f7d61: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen37174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37175" type="x-p"/> Then began he to upbraid the cities - The more God has done to draw men unto himself, the less excusable are they if they continue in iniquity. If our blessed Lord had not done every thing that was necessary for the salvation of these people, he could not have reproached them for their impenitence.
entries.40ccb15a8384390e214a13a3a2cf7076386c9ab4: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen37175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37176" type="x-p"/> Wo unto thee, Chorazin - Bethsaida! - It would be better to translate the word ουαι σοι, alas for thee, than wo to thee. The former is an exclamation of pity; the latter a denunciation of wrath. It is evident that our Lord used it in the former sense. It is not known precisely where Chorazin was situated; but as Christ joins it in the same censure with Bethsaida, which was in Upper Galilee, beyond the sea, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.45">Mar 6:45</reference>, it is likely that Chorazin was in the same quarter. Though the people in these cities were (generally) impenitent, yet there is little doubt that several received the word of life. Indeed, Bethsaida itself furnished not less than three of the twelve apostles, Philip, Andrew, and Peter.
